content.text: Can we explore what a richer metadata experience would look like using Hardcover/Goodreads metadata? It could be nice to be able to show sort of a richer set of metadata. For example, when you're looking at a book, you'd be able to click on the author and see things from that author, or you'd be able to click on, like, it would suggest similar books, maybe from your library, maybe from the market. I'm just wondering, like, is there a way that we could make the metadata a little bit better and then use that richer metadata to provide a better user experience? So I want you to kind of dig in and investigate what's feasible here.

Update the status and notes for each phase as work lands, so any agent can pick up from here. ## Goal First boot shows a setup screen that creates the admin. After that, signed-in users see their library (books on the filesystem, with metadata). An admin-only settings page manages users. Book metadata comes from the file itself, with online matching. ## Decisions (approved) - **Login by username only.** Better Auth `username` plugin. Better Auth still requires an email, so store a synthetic `@bookserve.local` and never show it. - **Roles** via the Better Auth `admin` plugin (`admin` / `user`). Settings is admin-only, enforced on the server. - **One library directory** for now (`BOOKSERVE_LIBRARY_DIR`), with a schema that allows more later. - **Paths from env:** `BOOKSERVE_DATA_DIR` (SQLite DB, covers, generated secret) and `BOOKSERVE_LIBRARY_DIR`. Dev defaults live under `./data`; the container uses `/config` and `/books`. - **Boot is self-sufficient:** create directories, run Drizzle migrations, and generate and persist the auth secret if none is set. - **Metadata:** read embedded EPUB metadata and cover on scan. Online matching is manual (as in Audiobookshelf). Open Library comes first (no key), then Google Books (optional key). Hardcover is later and optional. Matched metadata and covers are stored in the DB and data dir, never written into book files. Priority is two layers only: embedded EPUB metadata, then matched fields on top. No sidecar files (`metadata.opf`, `metadata.json`) and no metadata parsed from folder names. - **Dependencies for scanning:** `fflate` (unzip) + `fast-xml-parser` (OPF). Both are pure JS. EPUB first; PDF later. - **Uploads** are saved to `///<file>`. This is the only place the app writes into the library. ## Phases ### Phase 1 — Foundation and first-run setup — status: done - Config module for env paths and defaults. - Startup: create directories, run migrations, persist the generated secret. - Better Auth wired to Drizzle (SQLite) with the `username` and `admin` plugins; auth schema in `src/db/schema.ts`; committed migration. Remove the demo `todos` table. - `/setup` only when there are zero users: it creates the admin, then signs in. Otherwise it redirects. - `/login`. Every app route requires a session. - Dockerfile (multi-arch, `better-sqlite3` native build) plus a `.dockerignore`. ### Phase 2 — App shell and user management — status: done - Layout with Library (`/`) and Settings (`/settings`) navigation, plus sign-out. - `/settings/users` (admin only): list, add (username, password, role), change role, delete, reset password. ### Phase 3 — Library scanning and the grid view — status: done - `books` / `book_files` tables. - Scanner: walk the library directory for `.epub`, read OPF metadata and the cover (cached into the data dir), and handle added, moved, or removed files. Runs on startup and on demand (an admin button). - Library grid of covers; book detail page; download/stream the file. - Upload an EPUB into the library. ### Phase 4 — Online metadata matching — status: done - Provider interface; Open Library and Google Books providers with timeouts (the app works offline). - On the book detail page, "Match" searches, lists candidates, and lets the user choose fields to apply. Covers are cached on disk. ### Phase 5 — Market — status: done - An admin-only Market page for browsing online catalogs and adding books to the library, through pluggable integrations (`docs/market-integrations.md`): a bespoke Project Gutenberg integration (the default source) and a generic OPDS one. - Settings → Market sources to add and remove sources. Books added from the Market record their source in `book_sources`. - The Market searches and browses all sources at once, merging duplicate books, rows and shelves. ### Later In-browser reader, Market integrations loaded from `<data>/plugins/`, editing a source's settings, OPDS 2.0 (JSON) feed, OPDS browsing by author/series, Hardcover provider, file watching, PDF metadata, multiple libraries. Series from providers (neither Open Library search nor Google Books returns a usable series name). Edit metadata by hand (the same `books.matched` overlay). ## Notes log Append short notes here: gotchas, conventions established, verification commands. ### Phase 1 - **Config:** `src/lib/config.ts` (`dataDir`, `libraryDir`, `databasePath`, `secretPath`, `migrationsDir`, `publicUrl`). Server-only; read paths from here, never from `process.env` directly. - **Startup:** `src/server/startup.ts` is a Nitro plugin (registered in `vite.config.ts`) that imports `#/lib/auth`, which imports `#/db`. `src/db/index.ts` creates the data and library dirs, opens SQLite (WAL, foreign keys on), and runs the drizzle migrator; `src/lib/auth.ts` loads `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET` or creates `<data>/secret`. This runs at boot in both `pnpm dev` and `node .output/server/index.mjs`. Hook later startup work (e.g. the Phase 3 scan) into the same plugin. - **One DB connection:** Nitro's plugin bundle and the SSR bundle each include `src/db`, so the drizzle instance is cached on `globalThis.bookserveDb`. After changing the schema in dev, restart `pnpm dev`. - **Migrations:** edit `src/db/schema.ts`, run `pnpm db:generate --name <change>`, and commit `drizzle/`. They are read from `./drizzle` relative to the working directory (the repo root, or `/app` in the image, where the Dockerfile copies them). Don't use `db:push`. - **Auth tables** in `src/db/schema.ts` are hand-written to match Better Auth 1.7 with the `username` and `admin` plugins. If you add a Better Auth plugin that needs fields, add them there and generate a migration. - **Base URL:** `BOOKSERVE_URL` sets a fixed base URL (Secure cookies when https). Update the status and notes for each phase as work lands, so any agent can pick up from here. ## Goal First boot shows a setup screen that creates the admin. After that, signed-in users see their library (books on the filesystem, with metadata). An admin-only settings page manages users. Book metadata comes from the file itself, with online matching. ## Decisions (approved) - **Login by username only.** Better Auth `username` plugin. Better Auth still requires an email, so store a synthetic `@bookserve.local` and never show it. - **Roles** via the Better Auth `admin` plugin (`admin` / `user`). Settings is admin-only, enforced on the server. - **One library directory** for now (`BOOKSERVE_LIBRARY_DIR`), with a schema that allows more later. - **Paths from env:** `BOOKSERVE_DATA_DIR` (SQLite DB, covers, generated secret) and `BOOKSERVE_LIBRARY_DIR`. Dev defaults live under `./data`; the container uses `/config` and `/books`. - **Boot is self-sufficient:** create directories, run Drizzle migrations, and generate and persist the auth secret if none is set. - **Metadata:** read embedded EPUB metadata and cover on scan. Online matching is manual (as in Audiobookshelf). Open Library comes first (no key), then Google Books (optional key). Hardcover is later and optional. Matched metadata and covers are stored in the DB and data dir, never written into book files. Priority is two layers only: embedded EPUB metadata, then matched fields on top. No sidecar files (`metadata.opf`, `metadata.json`) and no metadata parsed from folder names. - **Dependencies for scanning:** `fflate` (unzip) + `fast-xml-parser` (OPF). Both are pure JS. EPUB first; PDF later. - **Uploads** are saved to `///<file>`. This is the only place the app writes into the library. ## Phases ### Phase 1 — Foundation and first-run setup — status: done - Config module for env paths and defaults. - Startup: create directories, run migrations, persist the generated secret. - Better Auth wired to Drizzle (SQLite) with the `username` and `admin` plugins; auth schema in `src/db/schema.ts`; committed migration. Remove the demo `todos` table. - `/setup` only when there are zero users: it creates the admin, then signs in. Otherwise it redirects. - `/login`. Every app route requires a session. - Dockerfile (multi-arch, `better-sqlite3` native build) plus a `.dockerignore`. ### Phase 2 — App shell and user management — status: done - Layout with Library (`/`) and Settings (`/settings`) navigation, plus sign-out. - `/settings/users` (admin only): list, add (username, password, role), change role, delete, reset password. ### Phase 3 — Library scanning and the grid view — status: done - `books` / `book_files` tables. - Scanner: walk the library directory for `.epub`, read OPF metadata and the cover (cached into the data dir), and handle added, moved, or removed files. Runs on startup and on demand (an admin button). - Library grid of covers; book detail page; download/stream the file. - Upload an EPUB into the library. ### Phase 4 — Online metadata matching — status: done - Provider interface; Open Library and Google Books providers with timeouts (the app works offline). - On the book detail page, "Match" searches, lists candidates, and lets the user choose fields to apply. Covers are cached on disk. ### Phase 5 — Market — status: done - An admin-only Market page for browsing online catalogs and adding books to the library, through pluggable integrations (`docs/market-integrations.md`): a bespoke Project Gutenberg integration (the default source) and a generic OPDS one. - Settings → Market sources to add and remove sources. Books added from the Market record their source in `book_sources`. - The Market searches and browses all sources at once, merging duplicate books, rows and shelves. ### Later In-browser reader, Market integrations loaded from `<data>/plugins/`, editing a source's settings, OPDS 2.0 (JSON) feed, OPDS browsing by author/series, Hardcover provider, file watching, PDF metadata, multiple libraries. Series from providers (neither Open Library search nor Google Books returns a usable series name). The temp file is always removed. - **UI:** `src/routes/_app/index.tsx` (grid, search, admin Scan/Upload buttons; missing books are dimmed and grayscale), `src/routes/_app/books/$bookId.tsx` (detail; "File missing" disabled button for missing books). `BookCover` (`src/components/book-cover.tsx`) renders the image or a placeholder tinted by a hash of the title. Fonts are the system stack (no Google Fonts). - **Test data:** ```bash mkdir -p .amp/in/epubs && cd .amp/in/epubs for id in 1342.epub3.images 84.epub3.images 2701.epub.images 11.epub.noimages; do curl -sSL -o "$id.epub" "https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/$id"; done head -c 2000 /dev/urandom > corrupt.epub ``` All four Gutenberg files currently ship a cover (including `11.epub.noimages`), so for the placeholder build a minimal EPUB without one (`mimetype`, `META-INF/container.xml`, an OPF with `calibre:series` and an HTML `dc:description`; a few lines of Python `zipfile`). Nest files in subfolders, then run the fresh-boot test with `BOOKSERVE_LIBRARY_DIR` pointing at the folder. - **Verification (Phase 3):** `pnpm lint`, `pnpm typecheck`, `pnpm build`; fresh boot on port 3100 with Playwright from `.amp/in/`: startup scan imports 4 books and skips the corrupt file; add a file + Scan → added; `mv` a file → same book id; `rm` → `missing = 1`; library dir moved away + Scan → error shown, nothing marked missing; upload via the file input (including a 120 MB file and an invalid one → inline error) → lands under `<Author>/<Title>/`; downloads match `shasum -a 256`; cover/download/upload → 401 without a session; scan server function → `Forbidden` and upload → 403 with a user's cookie; `..` and encoded-slash ids → 404. Docker: `docker run -v $T/config:/config -v $T/books:/books`, and `--tmpfs /config` to force the cross-device copy path. ### Phase 4 - **Providers** (`src/lib/metadata/`): `providers.ts` is client-safe (no server imports) and holds `PROVIDERS` (id + display name), the `Candidate`/`MatchFields`/`MetadataQuery` types and the `MetadataProvider` interface: `search(query) → Candidate[]` (one request; throws an `Error` whose message is shown inline as "<Provider>: <message>") and optional `details(id) → Partial<MatchFields>` for fields the search leaves out (the candidate sets `partial: true`; the dialog calls it when the candidate is picked). `http.ts` has `fetchJson` (8 s `AbortSignal.timeout`, `User-Agent: Bookserve/1.0 (...)`, errors become "Timed out" / "Could not connect" / `HttpError` with the status) and `downloadCover` (http(s) only, 15 s, 10 MB cap enforced while streaming, `image/jpeg|png|webp` content type _and_ magic bytes, so never SVG). - **Open Library** (`open-library.ts`): one `search.json` request (title + author, or `isbn` alone) with `fields=` including `editions,editions.publisher,editions.isbn,editions.language`: results are works, and publisher/ISBN/language come from the best-matching edition (the work's own lists span every edition). Published date is `first_publish_year`, covers are `covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/<cover_i>-L.jpg` (`-M` for thumbnails). `details` fetches `/works/<OL…W>.json` for the description (Markdown emphasis/links stripped, then `htmlToText`). - **Google Books** (`google-books.ts`): `volumes?q=intitle:… inauthor:…` or `isbn:…`, `key` from `config.googleBooksApiKey` (`GOOGLE_BOOKS_API_KEY`). Largest `imageLinks` entry, `http:` → `https:`, `&edge=curl` dropped; descriptions through `htmlToText` (exported from `src/lib/epub.ts`). **Keyless requests currently always get 429** (Google's shared keyless project has a daily quota of 0); the provider reports "Quota exceeded; set GOOGLE_BOOKS_API_KEY". - **Adding a provider** (e.g. Hardcover): add `{ id, name }` to `PROVIDERS`, write `src/lib/metadata/<name>.ts` exporting a `MetadataProvider` (use `fetchJson`; read any key through `src/lib/config.ts`), and register it in `IMPLEMENTATIONS` in `src/lib/match-functions.ts`. The dialog, provider select and per-provider errors pick it up from `PROVIDERS`. Hardcover is GraphQL with a bearer token: `fetchJson` only does GET, so give it a POST variant with the same timeout/User-Agent handling. - **Server functions** (`src/lib/match-functions.ts`, all `requireAdmin()`): `searchMetadata({ provider, query })` (one provider per call, so the dialog fires one per provider and renders each as it answers), `getMatchDetails({ provider, id })`, `applyMatch({ bookId, provider, providerId, fields, coverUrl })` and `revertMatch(bookId)`. `applyMatch` keeps only well-formed non-empty fields (`cleanFields`), merges them over the existing `books.matched` and records `source: { provider, id, matchedAt }`. Never called from the scanner. - **Matched covers:** `<data>/covers/<bookId>-matched.<ext>` (`matched.coverPath`); the scanner's `<bookId>.<ext>` is never touched (its cleanup only matches `<bookId>.`). A new matched cover replaces the previous matched file; `revertMatch` sets `matched = null` and deletes `<bookId>-matched.*`. The update bumps `updatedAt`, so the cover URL's `?v=` changes and the immutable-cached route serves the new image without a hard refresh. - **`MatchedMetadata`** gained `pageCount` (matching only; `bookView()` returns it, the detail page shows "Pages") and `source`. JSON column, so no migration. `getBook` returns `matched: boolean` for the revert button. - **UI:** `src/components/match-dialog.tsx` (search form prefilled from the view: title, first author, ISBN; provider select; results interleaved across providers; compare table with a checkbox per field, default checked when the new value is non-empty and differs, comparing displayed text so `en`/`eng` both read "English"; description row waits on `details`). Detail page: admin-only "Match" and, when matched, "Revert to file metadata" (confirm). `languageName` moved to `#/lib/utils`. - **Nav:** nav items take `also: '/books/'` to be active under another prefix (Library on book pages), via a `data-also-active` attribute next to TanStack's `data-status`. - **Verification (Phase 4):** `pnpm lint`, `pnpm typecheck`, `pnpm build`; fresh boot on port 3100 with 3 Gutenberg EPUBs and Playwright from `.amp/in/`. Google Books was served by a local mock (temporary `process.env` override of its `BASE_URL`, removed afterwards) because keyless requests get 429. Checked: both providers' results listed; apply with Authors and Published unchecked changes only the checked fields on the detail page and grid; the cover `?v=` changes and the served bytes equal `covers/<id>-matched.jpg`, scanned cover file kept; `touch` + Scan ("Updated …") keeps the matched fields and cover; revert restores title/cover (same sha as before) and deletes the matched file; Open Library pointed at `http://10.255.255.1` → "Open Library: Timed out" inline after 8 s while Google results show (and live: "Google Books: Quota exceeded; set GOOGLE_BOOKS_API_KEY" next to Open Library results); a user sees no Match button, and replaying `searchMetadata`/`getMatchDetails`/`applyMatch`/`revertMatch` with their cookie returns `Forbidden` (same replay with an admin cookie returns results). `downloadCover` checked against PNG (ok), SVG, SVG served as `image/jpeg`, 12 MB, 404, a hanging server (15 s) and `file://`. ### Phase 5 - **Integrations** (`src/lib/market/`): `sdk.ts` is the contract (`MarketIntegration`, `defineIntegration`, the `BookSummary`/`BookDetails`/`Listing`/`Home` types and `IntegrationContext`). `host.ts` registers the built-ins in `INTEGRATIONS`, builds each source's context (`ctx.fetch` with a 15 s timeout and the User-Agent, throwing `HttpError` on non-2xx; `ctx.cached`, an in-memory TTL cache per source id, at most 200 entries, failures not cached) and cleans all output (`cleanHome`/`cleanListing`/`cleanDetails`: trimmed strings, http(s) covers, date format, numeric sizes). `opds.ts` is a pure OPDS 1.x parser (`parseFeed`, `parseOpenSearch`, `fillSearchTemplate`). The author guide is `docs/market-integrations.md`. Integrations are built in for now; third-party loading comes later. - **Gutenberg** (`integrations/gutenberg.ts`), facts as of Nov 2026: no ISBNs; list feeds link each book to `/ebooks/<n>.opds`, whose feed has one entry per build (with and without images), each with EPUB links that carry `length`; covers are `cache/epub/<n>/pg<n>.cover.medium.jpg` (so lists need no extra request); downloads are `/ebooks/<n>.epub3.images|epub.images|epub.noimages`; audiobooks (e.g. 26301) have no EPUB; the description is the "Summary:" paragraph of the entry's content; `<published>` is Gutenberg's release date, so `publishedDate` is null. Author and subject **search** feeds (`/ebooks/authors/search.opds`) return 403 to non-browsers, so they're dropped; `/ebooks/author/<n>.opds`, `/ebooks/subject/<n>.opds` and `/ebooks/bookshelf/<n>.opds` work and come from a book's `rel="related"` links (shown as chips in the dialog). Home = Popular and Latest rows plus the "Category:" bookshelves 634–649. In lists, `<content>` is the author ("Jane Austen"), or "N downloads" when there is none. Shelf ids and cursors are paths, checked to stay under `https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/`. - **Generic OPDS** (`integrations/opds.ts`): settings `url` (required), `username`, `password` (HTTP Basic, sent only to the URL's origin; Node's fetch drops `Authorization` on cross-origin redirects). Shelf ids and cursors are feed URLs; book ids are `<feed URL>#<entry id>` and `book()` refetches that feed through the cache; format ids are download hrefs, checked against the entry. Entries with EPUB links are books, entries with a feed link are shelves. Search uses the root feed's `rel="search"` (Atom template or OpenSearch description). On Gutenberg's own OPDS root every book is a shelf, which is why Gutenberg has a bespoke integration. - **Schema** (migration `0002_market`): `market_sources` (`id`, `integration`, `name`, `settings` JSON, `created_at`; the migration inserts Project Gutenberg) and `book_sources` (`book_id` PK → books, cascade; `source_id` → market_sources, set null so provenance survives removing a source; `integration`; `external_id`; index on `(source_id, external_id)`). - **Server functions** (`src/lib/market-functions.ts`, all `requireAdmin()`): `listMarketSources` (password-type settings stripped), `listIntegrations`, `addMarketSource` (validates required and URL fields, then runs `check()` or `home()` with a throwaway cache; "Could not connect: …"), `removeMarketSource`, `marketBrowse({ sourceId, q?, shelf?, cursor? })` (one source's home or listing plus `inLibrary`, `<sourceId>:<externalId>` → library book id), `marketBook`, `marketAdd({ sourceId, bookId, formatId })`. `marketAdd` returns the existing book when the source already added that external id; otherwise it streams the download (10 min timeout) into `uploadBook`, inserts `book_sources`, and fills `books.matched` with only the fields the EPUB lacks (description, language, publisher, date, ISBN; the cover only when the EPUB has none) with `source: { provider: <integration>, id: <external id> }`. - **UI:** `src/routes/_app/market.tsx` (search params `q`, which goes through `String()` because the router parses `?q=123` as a number, and `shelf`, a JSON array of `{ source, id }`): home rows scroll horizontally, listings have a breadcrumb, shelf cards, a cover grid and "Load more"; the book dialog loads details when opened (format select with sizes, description, related shelf chips). `src/routes/_app/settings/market.tsx` (table, add dialog built from the integration's `settings`, remove confirm). `BookCover` falls back to the placeholder when an image fails to load. - **All sources at once** (`src/lib/market/merge.ts`): the page (`useMarket` in `market.tsx`) calls `marketBrowse` once per source and merges results as they arrive, so a slow source (15 s timeout) holds up only itself; errors show per source, and a failed "Load more" keeps that source's cursor. Listings merge page by page, so later pages never reorder earlier ones. Books merge on ISBN-13 (ISBN-10 converted; malformed ISBNs ignored), checked before title matches, or on `work:<title before :;([ or " - ", folded, leading article dropped>|<first author's surname: dates, parentheses and Jr./Sr. dropped, last word, so "Le Guin, Ursula" = "Ursula K. Le Guin">`; books without an author match only by ISBN; copies with different `language`s never merge. A book never takes two offers from one source (different editions of a work, e.g. Gutenberg's several Pride and Prejudice, stay apart). Results and each book's offers are in rank order across sources. Home rows merge by `kind` (`popular`, `new`; Gutenberg's Popular/Latest, an OPDS catalog's `sort/popular` and `sort/new` feeds) or folded title, shelves by folded title (`&` = "and"); on home a work merges across all rows. "In library" is one map for the page, so adding a book updates every card for it. The dialog loads details from every offer (reloading only when the offers change, keeping the chosen format); its format select lists all of them as "Source · label · size". A card's "Add" tries each offer's first format in order and shows the last error if none works. - **SDK** (after building Gutenberg and OPDS): `ctx.fetch` takes `method`/`body` and only http(s) URLs; `download()` returns the `Response` (e.g. `ctx.fetch(url)`), fetched with a 10 min timeout context; integrations import only from `sdk.ts`, which re-exports the OPDS parser and `htmlToText`. `apiVersion` stays 1: no integrations outside this repo existed yet. No fuzzy matching: "Frankenstein" vs "Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus" merge only because of the `;` cut. - **Verification (per-source loading, merge fixes):** merge cases checked with a scratch script (ISBN beats an earlier title match; Le Guin, King Jr., dated authors; curly quotes; malformed ISBNs; languages; offer and page order; `existing` not mutated). In the browser with a local OPDS catalog (popular/new feeds, a 5 s search): its "Most read" and "Just added" merged into Popular and Latest; "Dracula (Illustrated)" by "Bram Stoker (1847-1912)" merged with Gutenberg's Dracula; adding Gutenberg's "EPUB 2 without images" from the dialog wrote source 1 / 345 and the card turned "In library" without reload; search showed Gutenberg's results while the catalog was still loading, then merged it in; a Moby Dick whose catalog download 404s fell through to Gutenberg 2701 from the card; the merged sci-fi shelf's "Load more" kept The Time Machine once; with the catalog stopped, "Could not load Test Library: Could not connect" above Gutenberg's results. - **Verification (all sources, first version):** a local OPDS catalog (`python3 -m http.server`) with P&P by "Austen, Jane", Frankenstein, Emma and a "Science Fiction & Fantasy" shelf, added next to Gutenberg. Home: a "Test Library" row whose P&P shows "In library" (added from Gutenberg); the two sci-fi shelves merged into one tile, whose listing has The Time Machine once and "Load more" adding 50 Gutenberg books. Search "pride": the test copy merged into Gutenberg's first P&P, Emma from the test catalog. Frankenstein's format select: three Gutenberg formats and "Test Library · EPUB"; adding the latter wrote `book_sources` with `source_id` 3 and showed "In library" in both rows after reload. With the catalog stopped, search showed "Could not load Test Library: Could not connect" above Gutenberg's results. - **Verification (Phase 5):** `pnpm lint`, `pnpm typecheck`, `pnpm build`. Migration upgrade from 0000–0001 with a book row: Gutenberg seeded, deleting the source sets `source_id` null, deleting the book removes its `book_sources` row. Fresh `./data` in the browser: home rows and categories; search "jane austen" and "Load more" (50 results); Pride and Prejudice dialog (Summary, EPUB 3 · 24.9 MB default) → added under `Jane Austen/Pride and Prejudice/`, `book_sources` row, `matched.description` filled, cover from the EPUB kept, "In library" after reload; audiobook 26301 → "No EPUB available"; author chip → `/ebooks/author/68.opds` shelf; adding `https://example.com/` as OPDS → "Could not connect: Not an OPDS catalog"; `https://m.gutenberg.org/ebooks.opds/` added, browsed, removed. ### OPDS server - **Catalog** (`src/lib/opds-feed.ts`, routes in `src/routes/opds/`): OPDS 1.2 Atom. `/opds` is a navigation feed (Recently added, All books); `/opds/books` is the acquisition feed (`?sort=new`, `?q=` where every word must appear in the title, an author, the series or the ISBN, `?page=`, 50 per page, with first/last/previous/next links); `/opds/search` is the OpenSearch description, whose template is absolute (`BOOKSERVE_URL`, else X-Forwarded-Proto/Host, else the request). Books with `missing` are left out. Every book goes through `bookView`, so matched metadata and covers show. Entries link to the existing `/api/books/$id/cover` and `/download`; other hrefs are root-relative. - **Auth:** `requestUser(request)` in `src/lib/auth.ts` accepts a session cookie or HTTP Basic with the username and an API key as the password (see API keys below). `unauthorized()` sends `WWW-Authenticate: Basic`. The OPDS, cover and download routes use both. - **Verification:** `pnpm lint`, `pnpm typecheck`, `pnpm build`; seeded dev data with curl: 401 + challenge without/with wrong credentials, unknown user, banned user; feeds parsed by our own Market OPDS parser (`parseFeed`/`parseOpenSearch`/`fillSearchTemplate`, so a Bookserve can be another Bookserve's Market source); download sha256 equals the library file; cookie sessions still work for UI routes; 60 extra rows titled with `<b>&"` and U+0001 gave two well-formed pages (50 + 10), clamped `page=99`. ### API keys and KOSync - **API keys** (`api_keys`, `src/lib/api-key-functions.ts`, page `/settings/api-keys`, the one Settings section open to every user; the others hide from non-admins and redirect them to it): a named key per device, shown once. 20 characters from `a-z2-9` without look-alikes (~99 bits) in groups of five, because they're typed on e-reader keyboards. Only `sha256(md5(key))` is stored: KOSync clients send `md5(password)`, and a key used as a Basic password is md5'd to the same value. `apiKeyUser(username, md5Key)` in `src/lib/auth.ts` is one indexed lookup, so keys need no throttling or slow hashing. Keys are the only Basic credential; account passwords work only for the web sign-in. Deleting a key or the user revokes it. - **KOSync** (`src/routes/kosync/$.ts`, one splat route so any other path is a JSON 404): KOReader's Progress sync protocol under `/kosync`, following koreader-sync-server as written up in [kosync-conformance](https://github.com/pid1/kosync-conformance/blob/main/SPEC.md). `x-auth-user` + `x-auth-key` (md5 of an API key); `POST /users/create` refuses with 402/2005 and a message to use an API key; `GET /users/auth`; `PUT /syncs/progress` (last write wins, server timestamp in seconds); `GET /syncs/progress/:document` (`200 {}` when unknown). The `Accept` header isn't required. Document ids must match `[A-Za-z0-9_]{1,64}`, so nothing is stored that GET can't serve. Not implemented: healthcheck, `DELETE /users/me`, `PUT /users/password` (KOReader never calls them; accounts are Bookserve's). - **Progress** (`reading_progress`): keyed by user and the client's document id, so books outside the library sync too. The scanner stores KOReader's partial MD5 (`book_files.koreader_hash`: 1 KiB samples at 0 and `1024 << 2i`, i = 0..10) for new and changed files and backfills it for unchanged ones, so the book page shows the user's latest position (percentage, device, date). Only KOReader's default "Binary" matching links to a book; "Filename" matching still syncs between devices. - **KOReader sync page** (`/settings/sync`, `src/lib/sync-functions.ts`, open to every user): the server URL, and the user's synced positions, newest first, with book (linked when the hash matches a library file, else "Not in library"), percentage, device and date. KOReader's optional "Send document metadata" adds `metadata` (filename, title, authors) to each push; `reading_progress.metadata` keeps those string fields (trimmed, 500 chars each), a push without it leaves the stored one alone, and the page shows the title (else filename) for books outside the library. Reset deletes the server's row; readers keep their local position and the next push stores a new one. Admins get an Enabled switch (`kosyncEnabled` in `settings`); while off, every `/kosync` request gets 503/2000, not 401, so readers keep their credentials. - **Verification:** `pnpm lint`, `pnpm typecheck`, `pnpm build`. `koreaderHash` matches every synthetic vector in kosync-conformance and KOReader's own `leaves.epub` digest (`59d481d1…`). Upgrade from an install seeded on 0000–0002: migration applied and all 11 files got a hash on the startup scan. `verify.mjs --registration-off --no-healthcheck` with a second user: 46 passed, 0 failed (including cross-user isolation). In the browser as a non-admin: created a key, OPDS 200 with it, 401 with a wrong key or another user's name, password still 200; pushed a position for Frankenstein's downloaded file and its page showed 42% · Kobo Libra 2; deleting the key made KOSync and OPDS 401. Fresh data dir on the production build: tables created, `/kosync/users/auth` 401.

Getting Started with the API

Last Updated 5 days ago
Guide

Disclaimer:

...

To get an API token, you need to go to your account settings page and click on the Hardcover API link, then click the New API Key button.
Give your new token a memorable name to identify this use.

...

Set a time period for how long you want this token to be active for (Expiration). After that time the token will no longer work, and you’ll need to update it.

...

led “Rate Limits”
We have three distinct rate limits, which are designed to make the API as useful as possible.
* Daily Limit - You can see your Daily Limit, and your number of used requests, on your API Access page. Once you reach your Daily Limit, all requests will return a 429: Too Many Requests, try again later error.
* Per Minute Limit - How fast your per-minute rate refreshes.
* Burst Limit - The size of your token bucket.

...

Requests over it are rejected outright with a 403 ( request_exceeds_capacity ) rather than being rate-limited, because the bucket can never hold enough tokens. Split them into several requests.
Here are our current rate limits.
* Plan | Daily Limit | Burst Limit | Per Minute Limit | Intended Use
* Free | 5,000 | 10 | 60 | Personal ownership, progress sync, personal use, doing cool stuff

Readarr was the one app in my media stack I kept meaning to deal with. sqlite >  select  key ,  value  from  Config  where  key  =  'metadatasource' ; metadatasource|https: // api . bookinfo .pro
api.bookinfo.pro is the hosted instance of rreading-glasses, which its README describes as a drop-in replacement for Readarr’s defunct metadata service that “works with your existing installation” and is backwards-compatible with your library. It serves Goodreads-style data, or Hardcover data from a second endpoint.
So “Readarr is broken” wasn’t true for me. What is true is that Readarr will never get another release: no bug fixes, no security patches, nothing new.

# Getting Started with the API
## Getting an API Key
Section titled “Getting an API Key”
To get an API token, you need to go to your account settings page and click on the [Hardcover API](https://hardcover.app/account/api) link, then click the [New API Key](https://hardcover.app/account/api/keys/new) button.
Give your new token a memorable name to identify this use. If this is for a 3rd-party (ex: NickelHardcover, Hardcover KOReader Plugin), then using that as the token name can be helpful. Set a time period for how long you want this token to be active for (Expiration). After that time the token will no longer work, and you’ll need to update it.
Next, select which permissions you want to allow this token to access. Tokens created using the previous system (before August 2026) have access equivalent to `all` . The new setup allows for specifying the exact permissions this token needs. This helps prevent a rogue token or application you’re unfamiliar with from taking actions beyond what you’re comfortable with.
If you’re generating a token for a specific application, read through that applications permission requirements to see what it needs.
The API token creation screen asking for an optional label, expiration time and allowed scopes The API token creation screen asking for an optional label, expiration time and allowed scopes The box that appears when you create a new API token. Make sure you copy your token! The box that appears when you create a new API token. Make sure you copy your token!

...

If you are not making a simple script or a simple tool for yourself, and you want to make it easier for your users, then it is recommended to use OAuth.
OAuth lets your users not have to manually create tokens and give it the correct permissions your app requires, [Read more about OAuth](https://docs.hardcover.app/api/oauth) .
However, if you are building tools or scripts that have to use PATs, then check out the [PAT Link Builder](https://docs.hardcover.app/api/pat-link-builder) — it generates a link that opens the new key form with the scopes your app needs already checked, so your users don’t have to hunt through the list themselves.

...

## API Response Codes
| Code | Description | Example Body |
| 200 | The request was successful |  |
| 400 | Malformed request body, or an unparseable GraphQL query | `{ error: "Malformed request body" }` or `{ error: "invalid_query", error_description: "..." }` |
| 401 | Missing, invalid, or expired token | `{ error: "invalid_token", error_description: "..." }` |
| 403 | Missing scope, disallowed operation, a request with more top-level fields than your Burst Limit (see Rate Limits ), or no access to the requested resource | `{ error: "insufficient_scope", error_description: "...", scope: "..." }` (see note below) |
| 404 | Not Found |  |
| 408 | Query exceeded the max timeout | `{ error: "Request timeout" }` |
| 429 | Too Many Requests, try again later | `{ error: "Too Many Requests", message: "..." }` |
| 500 | Internal Server Error | `{ error: "An unknown error occurred" }` |
| 503 | Temporarily unavailable, safe to retry | `{ error: "Service temporarily unavailable" }` |

### Note:
Section titled “Note:”
A `403` can come with a few different `error` values depending on the cause:
* `insufficient_scope` - your token is missing a scope the query needs (also includes a `scope` field listing what’s missing)
* `unsupported_operation` - that operation isn’t available to API tokens
* `request_exceeds_capacity` - the request has more top-level fields than your Burst Limit (see Rate Limits ); comes back as `{ errors: ["request_exceeds_capacity"], message: "..." }` instead of a single `error`
* anything else - a plain `{ error: "<message>" }` describing why you don’t have access

...

## Important Notes About the Hardcover API
* The API is still heavily in flux right now. Anything you build using it could break in the future.
* We may reset tokens without notice while in beta.
* The same ownership rights exist for this as anything on the site.
+ You own your data.
+ This means you can’t use the API to access and use someone else’s data.
* This API is running the same as if you were using the browser. Any actions you take will be under your user.
* Don't share your token! Someone could delete your account with it.
* CORS is open, so requests from a web browser will work, but make sure you store your tokens securely. Anything your page sends is visible to anyone who opens devtools (or XSS on your site). A PAT can have a long expiration window and be used to delete the account outright with the `all` scope.
* For anything a user signs into, use [OAuth](https://docs.hardcover.app/api/oauth) : those tokens are short-lived, limited to the scopes you request and permit, and the user can easily revoke them. Never ask a user to paste a PAT into your app.
* Recommendation When authoring scripts that use the API, it is recommended to include a user-agent header with a description of the script.
* Queries have a max timeout of 30 seconds.
* By using the API, you agree not to use to train large language models that are made publicly available or used commercially.

## Commercial API Use
Section titled “Commercial API Use”
As mentioned on the [Hardcover Policies Page](https://hardcover.app/pages/policies) , we make no copyright or proprietary rights over this data, and it should be used at your own risk.
If you’re creating a commercial product, or making a publicly accessible website, you _may not use data owned by users_ . This includes, but is not limited to:
* Users libraries and stats
* User reviews, ratings, dates read
* Reading journal entries
* Prompts and prompt answers
* Lists and books on lists
* Vibes and vibe books
* User Goals
* User Network and activities
This data should not be accessed in the API by commerical products unless on behalf a user who has allowed their data to be accessed.
Using aggregate data is allowed, if it’s mentioned to be Hardcover data (ex: number of Hardcover Readers, average Hardcover rating).

...

### Public Data Warning
Images on Hardcover are uploaded by users on the internet. If you use any images from the API and those images are open to the public, make absolutely sure you have a [DMCA takedown policy](https://hardcover.app/pages/dmca) listed on your site. Without that, copyright holders may attempt to extort you with legal action (this has happened to us, and this policy protected us). If you’re running a full commerical site, I’d recommend also registering a DMCA Agent.

...

## Limitations
* The following queries are disabled:
  + `_like`
  + `_nlike`
  + `_ilike`
  + `_niregex`
  + `_nregex`
  + `_iregex`
  + `_regex`
  + `_nsimilar`
  + `_similar`
* Queries have a max timeout of 30 seconds.
* Search queries have a max timeout of 2 seconds.
* Queries are not allowed to run in the browser, they must be run in an environment where the token can be kept secure.

## Rate Limits
Section titled “Rate Limits”
We have three distinct rate limits, which are designed to make the API as useful as possible.
* **Daily Limit** - You can see your Daily Limit, and your number of used requests, on your [API Access](https://hardcover.app/account/api) page. Once you reach your Daily Limit, all requests will return a `429: Too Many Requests, try again later` error.
* **Per Minute Limit** - How fast your per-minute rate refreshes.
* **Burst Limit** - The size of your token bucket.
You can fire off this many requests back-to-back before being throttled; it refills continuously at your Per Minute Limit.
+ Each top-level field in a request costs one token, so a single request can contain at most as many top-level fields as your Burst Limit. Requests over it are rejected outright with a `403` ( `request_exceeds_capacity` ) rather than being rate-limited, because the bucket can never hold enough tokens. Split them into several requests.
Here are our current rate limits.
| Plan | Daily Limit | Burst Limit | Per Minute Limit | Intended Use |
| `Free` | 5,000 | 10 | 60 | Personal ownership, progress sync, personal use, doing cool stuff |
| `Supporter` | 50,000 | 15 | 60 | Heavy data needs, always running processes, research |
These rate limits are intended to be plenty for the vast majority of use cases. If you’re running a **project for the public good** (ex: the Hardcover bot in /r/suggestmeabook on Reddit to fetch book info) that uses Hardcover and would like to have your rate increased, please reach out to **jules@hardcover.app** with information about your project, why you’re requesting a rate increase and what limit you would like to request.
If you’re running a **commercial product** (or one that intends to be a commercial product in the future) that requires higher API limits, you’re in luck! We’re building that out right now. Look for that in the near future.
Each top-level query within a GraphQL query counts as one request towards each of these limits (introspection fields such as `__typename` don’t count). For example, this request would count as 2 requests towards your limit.
```
query Test { me { username } m2:me { name } }
```

...

Personal Access Tokens get double the burst capacity of legacy JWT-based authentication on the same plan. If you’re still authenticating with a JWT, switching to a PAT (see Getting an API Key above) is an easy way to raise your burst ceiling.

### Rate Limit Headers
Section titled “Rate Limit Headers”
The API will always respond with rate limiting headers describing your current rate limit state, so you can back off proactively instead of waiting for a `429` .

#### `RateLimit` headers
Section titled “RateLimit headers”
* **`RateLimit-Policy`** - the limits that apply to your token, one entry per bucket:
`"Free";q=60;w=60;burst=10, "daily";q=5000;w=86400`
+ `Free` - The plan name for this token
+ `q` - quota (requests per window)
+ `w` - window length, in seconds
+ `burst` - max burst size for that bucket (only present on the per-minute bucket)
* **`RateLimit`** - your current standing, in the same shape:
`"Free";r=8;t=0, "daily";r=4231;t=51234`
+ `r` - requests remaining
+ `t` - seconds until that bucket resets
The per-minute window will always be 60 seconds, so the quota will be your Per Minute Limit or how many evenly spaced requests you can do in a minute, and the burst is your Burst Limit or how many requests you can do at once.
So with the example policy above, you can make a quick 10 requests back to back before either having to switch to making 1 request per second, or waiting 10 seconds for your bucket to refill completely.
Tip
Your plan’s `r` is capped by your remaining daily requests, and once the daily limit is used up the plan entry is left out and only the `daily` entry is sent.
The `t` in the per-minute bucket is 0 while you have tokens left, and once it’s empty it will be seconds until slots are available; for `daily` it is the time until the reset (midnight UTC). You can take the minimum of both values to know how long you have to wait until you can make your next request.
Note
Curious why these headers look like `"Free";r=8;t=42` ?
They follow the [IETF RateLimit header fields draft](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers/) - check it out if you want the full spec.

#### `X-RateLimit-*` headers (legacy)
Section titled “X-RateLimit-* headers (legacy)”
| Header | Description |
| `X-RateLimit-Limit` | Your tier’s burst capacity (e.g. 10 for Free, 15 for Supporter) |
| `X-RateLimit-Remaining` | Requests remaining before you’re throttled - the stricter of your burst and daily remaining |
| `X-RateLimit-Reset` | Unix timestamp when your burst bucket refills |
| `X-RateLimit-Daily-Limit` | Your plan’s daily request cap |
| `X-RateLimit-Daily-Remaining` | Requests remaining today |
| `X-RateLimit-Daily-Reset` | Unix timestamp of your next daily reset (midnight UTC) |
Caution
These headers are kept for backward compatibility and may be removed once the `RateLimit` / `RateLimit-Policy` headers above are finalized as a published standard.
Build new integrations against those instead.

#### `Retry-After`
Section titled “Retry-After”
When a request is throttled ( `429` ), the response also includes a `Retry-After` header with the number of seconds you have to wait before you can make another request.

...

# Getting Started with the API
## Getting an API Key
Section titled “Getting an API Key”
To get an API token, you need to go to your account settings page and click on the [Hardcover API](https://hardcover.app/account/api) link, then click the [New API Key](https://hardcover.app/account/api/keys/new) button.
Give your new token a memorable name to identify this use. If this is for a 3rd-party (ex: NickelHardcover, Hardcover KOReader Plugin), then using that as the token name can be helpful. Set a time period for how long you want this token to be active for (Expiration). After that time the token will no longer work, and you’ll need to update it.
Next, select which permissions you want to allow this token to access. Tokens created using the previous system (before August 2026) have access equivalent to `all` . The new setup allows for specifying the exact permissions this token needs. This helps prevent a rogue token or application you’re unfamiliar with from taking actions beyond what you’re comfortable with.
If you’re generating a token for a specific application, read through that applications permission requirements to see what it needs.
The API token creation screen asking for an optional label, expiration time and allowed scopes The API token creation screen asking for an optional label, expiration time and allowed scopes The box that appears when you create a new API token. Make sure you copy your token! The box that appears when you create a new API token. Make sure you copy your token!

...

If you are not making a simple script or a simple tool for yourself, and you want to make it easier for your users, then it is recommended to use OAuth.
OAuth lets your users not have to manually create tokens and give it the correct permissions your app requires, [Read more about OAuth](https://docs.hardcover.app/api/oauth) .
However, if you are building tools or scripts that have to use PATs, then check out the [PAT Link Builder](https://docs.hardcover.app/api/pat-link-builder) — it generates a link that opens the new key form with the scopes your app needs already checked, so your users don’t have to hunt through the list themselves.

...

## API Response Codes
| Code | Description | Example Body |
| 200 | The request was successful |  |
| 400 | Malformed request body, or an unparseable GraphQL query | `{ error: "Malformed request body" }` or `{ error: "invalid_query", error_description: "..." }` |
| 401 | Missing, invalid, or expired token | `{ error: "invalid_token", error_description: "..." }` |
| 403 | Missing scope, disallowed operation, a request with more top-level fields than your Burst Limit (see Rate Limits ), or no access to the requested resource | `{ error: "insufficient_scope", error_description: "...", scope: "..." }` (see note below) |
| 404 | Not Found |  |
| 408 | Query exceeded the max timeout | `{ error: "Request timeout" }` |
| 429 | Too Many Requests, try again later | `{ error: "Too Many Requests", message: "..." }` |
| 500 | Internal Server Error | `{ error: "An unknown error occurred" }` |
| 503 | Temporarily unavailable, safe to retry | `{ error: "Service temporarily unavailable" }` |

### Note:
Section titled “Note:”
A `403` can come with a few different `error` values depending on the cause:
* `insufficient_scope` - your token is missing a scope the query needs (also includes a `scope` field listing what’s missing)
* `unsupported_operation` - that operation isn’t available to API tokens
* `request_exceeds_capacity` - the request has more top-level fields than your Burst Limit (see Rate Limits ); comes back as `{ errors: ["request_exceeds_capacity"], message: "..." }` instead of a single `error`
* anything else - a plain `{ error: "<message>" }` describing why you don’t have access

...

## Important Notes About the Hardcover API
* The API is still heavily in flux right now. Anything you build using it could break in the future.
* We may reset tokens without notice while in beta.
* The same ownership rights exist for this as anything on the site.
+ You own your data.
+ This means you can’t use the API to access and use someone else’s data.
* This API is running the same as if you were using the browser. Any actions you take will be under your user.
* Don't share your token! Someone could delete your account with it.
* CORS is open, so requests from a web browser will work, but make sure you store your tokens securely. Anything your page sends is visible to anyone who opens devtools (or XSS on your site). A PAT can have a long expiration window and be used to delete the account outright with the `all` scope.
* For anything a user signs into, use [OAuth](https://docs.hardcover.app/api/oauth) : those tokens are short-lived, limited to the scopes you request and permit, and the user can easily revoke them. Never ask a user to paste a PAT into your app.
* Recommendation When authoring scripts that use the API, it is recommended to include a user-agent header with a description of the script.
* Queries have a max timeout of 30 seconds.
* By using the API, you agree not to use to train large language models that are made publicly available or used commercially.

## Commercial API Use
Section titled “Commercial API Use”
As mentioned on the [Hardcover Policies Page](https://hardcover.app/pages/policies) , we make no copyright or proprietary rights over this data, and it should be used at your own risk.
If you’re creating a commercial product, or making a publicly accessible website, you _may not use data owned by users_ . This includes, but is not limited to:
* Users libraries and stats
* User reviews, ratings, dates read
* Reading journal entries
* Prompts and prompt answers
* Lists and books on lists
* Vibes and vibe books
* User Goals
* User Network and activities
This data should not be accessed in the API by commerical products unless on behalf a user who has allowed their data to be accessed.
Using aggregate data is allowed, if it’s mentioned to be Hardcover data (ex: number of Hardcover Readers, average Hardcover rating).

...

### Public Data Warning
Images on Hardcover are uploaded by users on the internet. If you use any images from the API and those images are open to the public, make absolutely sure you have a [DMCA takedown policy](https://hardcover.app/pages/dmca) listed on your site. Without that, copyright holders may attempt to extort you with legal action (this has happened to us, and this policy protected us). If you’re running a full commerical site, I’d recommend also registering a DMCA Agent.

...

## Limitations
* The following queries are disabled:
  + `_like`
  + `_nlike`
  + `_ilike`
  + `_niregex`
  + `_nregex`
  + `_iregex`
  + `_regex`
  + `_nsimilar`
  + `_similar`
* Queries have a max timeout of 30 seconds.
* Search queries have a max timeout of 2 seconds.
* Queries are not allowed to run in the browser, they must be run in an environment where the token can be kept secure.

## Rate Limits
Section titled “Rate Limits”
We have three distinct rate limits, which are designed to make the API as useful as possible.
* **Daily Limit** - You can see your Daily Limit, and your number of used requests, on your [API Access](https://hardcover.app/account/api) page. Once you reach your Daily Limit, all requests will return a `429: Too Many Requests, try again later` error.
* **Per Minute Limit** - How fast your per-minute rate refreshes.
* **Burst Limit** - The size of your token bucket.
You can fire off this many requests back-to-back before being throttled; it refills continuously at your Per Minute Limit.
+ Each top-level field in a request costs one token, so a single request can contain at most as many top-level fields as your Burst Limit. Requests over it are rejected outright with a `403` ( `request_exceeds_capacity` ) rather than being rate-limited, because the bucket can never hold enough tokens. Split them into several requests.
Here are our current rate limits.
| Plan | Daily Limit | Burst Limit | Per Minute Limit | Intended Use |
| `Free` | 5,000 | 10 | 60 | Personal ownership, progress sync, personal use, doing cool stuff |
| `Supporter` | 50,000 | 15 | 60 | Heavy data needs, always running processes, research |
These rate limits are intended to be plenty for the vast majority of use cases. If you’re running a **project for the public good** (ex: the Hardcover bot in /r/suggestmeabook on Reddit to fetch book info) that uses Hardcover and would like to have your rate increased, please reach out to **jules@hardcover.app** with information about your project, why you’re requesting a rate increase and what limit you would like to request.
If you’re running a **commercial product** (or one that intends to be a commercial product in the future) that requires higher API limits, you’re in luck! We’re building that out right now. Look for that in the near future.
Each top-level query within a GraphQL query counts as one request towards each of these limits (introspection fields such as `__typename` don’t count). For example, this request would count as 2 requests towards your limit.
```
query Test { me { username } m2:me { name } }
```

...

Personal Access Tokens get double the burst capacity of legacy JWT-based authentication on the same plan. If you’re still authenticating with a JWT, switching to a PAT (see Getting an API Key above) is an easy way to raise your burst ceiling.

### Rate Limit Headers
Section titled “Rate Limit Headers”
The API will always respond with rate limiting headers describing your current rate limit state, so you can back off proactively instead of waiting for a `429` .

#### `RateLimit` headers
Section titled “RateLimit headers”
* **`RateLimit-Policy`** - the limits that apply to your token, one entry per bucket:
`"Free";q=60;w=60;burst=10, "daily";q=5000;w=86400`
+ `Free` - The plan name for this token
+ `q` - quota (requests per window)
+ `w` - window length, in seconds
+ `burst` - max burst size for that bucket (only present on the per-minute bucket)
* **`RateLimit`** - your current standing, in the same shape:
`"Free";r=8;t=0, "daily";r=4231;t=51234`
+ `r` - requests remaining
+ `t` - seconds until that bucket resets
The per-minute window will always be 60 seconds, so the quota will be your Per Minute Limit or how many evenly spaced requests you can do in a minute, and the burst is your Burst Limit or how many requests you can do at once.
So with the example policy above, you can make a quick 10 requests back to back before either having to switch to making 1 request per second, or waiting 10 seconds for your bucket to refill completely.
Tip
Your plan’s `r` is capped by your remaining daily requests, and once the daily limit is used up the plan entry is left out and only the `daily` entry is sent.
The `t` in the per-minute bucket is 0 while you have tokens left, and once it’s empty it will be seconds until slots are available; for `daily` it is the time until the reset (midnight UTC). You can take the minimum of both values to know how long you have to wait until you can make your next request.
Note
Curious why these headers look like `"Free";r=8;t=42` ?
They follow the [IETF RateLimit header fields draft](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers/) - check it out if you want the full spec.

#### `X-RateLimit-*` headers (legacy)
Section titled “X-RateLimit-* headers (legacy)”
| Header | Description |
| `X-RateLimit-Limit` | Your tier’s burst capacity (e.g. 10 for Free, 15 for Supporter) |
| `X-RateLimit-Remaining` | Requests remaining before you’re throttled - the stricter of your burst and daily remaining |
| `X-RateLimit-Reset` | Unix timestamp when your burst bucket refills |
| `X-RateLimit-Daily-Limit` | Your plan’s daily request cap |
| `X-RateLimit-Daily-Remaining` | Requests remaining today |
| `X-RateLimit-Daily-Reset` | Unix timestamp of your next daily reset (midnight UTC) |
Caution
These headers are kept for backward compatibility and may be removed once the `RateLimit` / `RateLimit-Policy` headers above are finalized as a published standard.
Build new integrations against those instead.

#### `Retry-After`
Section titled “Retry-After”
When a request is throttled ( `429` ), the response also includes a `Retry-After` header with the number of seconds you have to wait before you can make another request.

...

## API Roadmap
* 2026 OAuth support will be added for external applications.
* 2026 Client-side API use will be supported
* 2026 Queries will have a maximum depth of 3.
* 2026 Queries may be limited to your own user data, public data, and user data of users you follow.

...

## Further Reading
Section titled “Further Reading”
* [GraphQL API Reference](https://graphql.org/learn/)

# OAuth
Last Updated   September 24, 2026
Guide
Personal Access Tokens are great for scripts and tools you run yourself.
You create the token, you paste it into your own config, only you ever see it.
But if you want other people to use your application or tool then OAuth is the way to go.

...

Everything below builds on the same [scopes](https://docs.hardcover.app/api/graphql/actions) as a Personal Access Token,
and once you do an OAuth flow and get an OAuth Access Token it works exactly like a PAT with the API,
the difference is entirely in how you get it.

...

## How it works
OAuth allows for a secure handshake between the auth provider (Hardcover) and your application by using the user as the courier.
There are 2 flows for OAuth we support, the standard flow ( [RFC6749](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749) ) and device authorization grant ( [RFC8628](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8628) ).

...

### Standard flow
1. Your app generate 2 random strings, one is the `state` and the other is the `code_verifier` for PKCE that you then SHA256 hash to get the `code_challenge` .
2. Your app sends the user to the authorize endpoint with your `client_id` , `redirect_uri` the place the user gets sent to after they finish on hardcover, the random `state` , and the PKCE `code_challenge` , and `scope` which is a subset of your allowed scopes.
3.
The user sees your app’s name, icon, and the scopes you’re asking for, and approves or denies.
4. Hardcover redirects back to your `redirect_uri` with a short-lived `code` (plus your `state` value, and an `iss` parameter naming the issuer).
5. Your app exchanges that code along with the PKCE `code_verifier` you generated in step 1 at the token endpoint for an access token and a refresh token.
6. Use the access token as a Bearer token against the API, exactly like a PAT.
This is the authorization code flow with PKCE, which we require every client use regardless of type.
There’s no separate “simpler” flow for a trusted client (and also no implicit grant).
So PKCE ( `code_challenge_method=S256` ) is required on every request, confidential clients included, it isn’t just for public clients.
Tip
Different clients can have slight differences from the flow described above, as it is the general steps for when you are a website, either SPA or SSR. For other types clients you will have to do some extra steps.
Desktop and CLI apps have to start a webserver and bind to a random localhost port after step 1 to catch the user when they return on the `redirect_uri` .
Hardcover accepts any port on localhost (and other loopback addresses) so you don’t have to worry if the port you wanted is already in use and you have to register another.

...

Mobile apps can set a custom scheme (instead of https) for the `redirect_uri` that will launch their app to collect the user. And when sending the user to Hardcover they can use a webview.
Note
Check that `state` matches what you sent in step 2 (this is what makes the flow safe from CSRF),
and check that `iss` equals `https://api.hardcover.app` before treating `code` or `state` as valid.
Hardcover only has one authorization server today, but the `iss` check is what stops a malicious server from ever being able to hand your app a code that gets redeemed at the wrong place (a “mix-up” attack ( [RFC9207](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9207) )).

...

### Device Authorization Grant
1. Your app requests a Device Auth Grant to start with your `client_id` , and optionally `scope` if you want a subset of your allowed scopes.
2. Hardcover gives your app a json object (see table below) that has info on where to send the user, what code the user should enter and how often you should poll.
3.
Your app starts polling the device auth endpoint at `interval` seconds until `expires_in` elapses, and sends the `device_code` so hardcover knows which request is being discussed.
4.
Your app tells the user to go to `verification_uri` ( [hardcover.app/link](https://hardcover.app/link) ) and enter `user_code` (it will be in the format of “ABCD-1234”), additionally you can turn `verification_uri_complete` into a QR code, that will take the user and prefill the code for them.
5. After the user enters the code the user sees your app’s name, icon, and the scopes you’re asking for, and approves or denies.
6.
Hardcover will respond to one of your poll requests with the access token and refresh token.
7. Use the access token as a Bearer token against the API, exactly like a PAT.
Response for device auth flow start (step 2)
| Field | Description |
| `device_code` | id you use to identify your polling requests |
| `user_code` | the code you tell the user to enter |
| `verification_uri` | where you tell the user to go |
| `verification_uri_complete` | a complete url you can turn to a QR that will prefill the code |
| `expires_in` | in seconds, how long you have to do the auth before giving up |
| `interval` | in seconds, how often you should poll |
Note
When turning `verification_uri_complete` into a QR code, make sure that you are still displaying the instructions using `verification_uri` and `user_code` in case the user can’t scan a QR code.
Caution

...

For the standard OAuth flow on public clients this is not as much of a issue, for websites Hardcover will only accept registered `redirect_uri` , so unless someone takes over your domain they can not start an OAuth flow in your name. But it can be an issue for CLI and desktop apps, so unless your app needs it don’t register a loopback address as an accepted `redirect_uri` .

...

## Which flow do I need?
| You’re building | Pick | Client type | Guide |
| A server-rendered app (Rails, Django, Node, PHP, etc.) or Backend-For-Frontend (BFF) server for an app, anything that runs on infrastructure you control | Web app (server-side) | Confidential: Gets a client secret, plus PKCE | [Confidential client guide](https://docs.hardcover.app/api/oauth/getting-started-server) |
| A React/Vue/Svelte app that runs in the user’s browser | Single-page app | Public: no secret, PKCE only | [SPA guide](https://docs.hardcover.app/api/oauth/getting-started-spa) |
| A mobile app, desktop app, CLI tool, or e-reader plugin | Mobile, desktop, or CLI | Public: no secret, PKCE only, Device Authorization Grant enabled, can have custom URI schemes in redirect | [Native / device guide](https://docs.hardcover.app/api/oauth/getting-started-device) |

...

### What is PKCE?
Section titled “What is PKCE?”
PKCE ( [RFC 7636](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7636) ) is an addition to the OAuth flow to make sure that the client that started the flow is the device that completed it.
By having the device make up a secret with at least 256 bits entropy ( `code_verifier` ) then send a SHA256 hashed version ( `code_challenge` ) of it to the server when starting the flow, the auth provider can be sure that only someone who can provide the code that hashes to the challenge it initially got is the correct device when doing the key exchange.

...

### Why should I disable Device Authorization Grant if I am not using it
Unlike the standard flows where even for Public apps the auth provider can only send the user to pre-approved `redirect_uri` s,
for Device Authorization Grant all you need is the apps public client id.
So if you don’t disable Device Auth Grant people will be able to take the client id that is embedded in your app, and in the standard flow is sent with the user, and start Auth flows with it in the name of your apps with whatever scopes have allowed for it.

...

## Endpoints
All of these (and the full set of grant types, scopes, and auth methods this server supports) are also published at the discovery document.
It is recommended that you make a call to discovery and read it at startup rather than hardcoding these if you can,
since if we ever have to change anything then your app can load in the new URLs automatically.
| Purpose | URL |
| Discovery | https://api.hardcover.app/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server |
| Token | `POST` https://api.hardcover.app/oauth2/token |
| Revoke | `POST` https://api.hardcover.app/oauth2/revoke |
| Introspect (confidential clients only) | `POST` https://api.hardcover.app/oauth2/introspect |
| Device authorization | `POST` https://api.hardcover.app/oauth2/device |
| Authorize (browser redirect) | https://hardcover.app/oauth2/authorize |
| Device verification (human-facing) | https://hardcover.app/link |

## Tokens
Section titled “Tokens”
Access and refresh tokens are opaque random strings, not JWTs. There’s nothing to decode client-side.
If you need to check whether a token is still valid, use the introspection endpoint (confidential clients only) or just try it against the API.
* **Access tokens** ( `hc_at_XXXXX` ) last 1 week and work exactly like a PAT for API requests.
* **Refresh tokens** ( `hc_rt_XXXXX` ) last 6 months, and **rotate on every use** .
Each refresh returns a new refresh token, and the one you just spent stops working.
If a refresh token ever gets used twice (yours got copied, or you’re retrying a request that actually succeeded),
the server treats it as a replay and revokes that token’s entire chain, making it so the user has to go through an OAuth flow again.
Your app should always save the newest refresh token and only ever use it once.

## Scopes
Section titled “Scopes”
OAuth apps use the same [scopes](https://docs.hardcover.app/api/graphql/actions) as Personal Access Tokens, but there are a some differences between them and PATs:
The scopes you list when registering your app are a cap, and are intersected with your requested scopes at consent time, that is then intersected with the user’s allowed scopes at request time.

...

When you make a request to the OAuth authorize endpoint you have to include the scopes you want, they are not implied from your allowed scopes.
But, it is possible to omit them when refreshing the token, you will then be issued a token with the same scopes as the last one.
You can also request any subset of the scopes the user consented to when refreshing without having to go through the OAuth flow again.

...

## Registering an app
| Field | What it’s for |
| Application type | Confidential vs. public, and can’t be changed later — see Which flow do I need . |
| Name | Shown to the user on the consent screen, and afterward in their list of connected apps. |
| Icon | Same as Name — consent screen and the connected apps list. |
| Description | Not currently shown at consent time — it only appears later, on the user’s connected apps list. Reserved for a future use (either added to the consent screen, or a future app directory style feature) — worth filling in for when that lands, even though it’s not surfaced yet. |
| Website URL | Shown as a link on the consent screen, right under your app’s name — it and the redirect host are the two things a user can actually verify, since `client_id` alone can be seen by anyone. |
| Redirect URIs | Where Hardcover sends the user back after they approve or deny. Must be `https` , except loopback addresses ( `127.0.0.1` , `[::1]` , `localhost` ) where it can be `http` — for local development or desktop apps. A custom URI scheme is possible for native apps. URIs are matched exactly — no wildcards or prefixes. |
| Device Authorization Grant toggle | Lets your app’s `client_id` be used at the device endpoint and `hardcover.app/link` . Off unless you turn it on (pre-checked for native apps, but still changeable). |
| Scopes this app may request | The ceiling described under Scopes above. Only ask for what you actually need, the app can request a subset of these at auth time, shown on the consent screen. |

...

## Consent and revoking access
Users manage every app they’ve connected from the [Authorized Apps](https://hardcover.app/account/api/authorized-apps) page.
Revoking an app there kills every token it holds for that user immediately, and clears their consent record — your app will need to send them through the authorize flow again from scratch, not just refresh.

...

## Storing tokens on the client
Section titled “Storing tokens on the client”

...

## Appearance in Authorized apps
* Active sessions are sessions where the Access Token is still valid and might be in use.
* Idle sessions are where the Access Token has expired, but the Refresh Token is still valid and can be used to reactivate the session.
On each of the sessions we store the last used User Agent and parse that to show a client name,
however it only parse out common user agents, and if it does not recognise the User Agent it will show up blank.
If you want your client to show correctly (e.g. ‘Softcover’ or ‘Hardcover.app for KOReader’) then reach out on discord!

...

## Compliance
Hardcover’s OAuth tries to be in compliance with the [OAuth 2.1 recommendations](https://oauth.net/2.1/) .
So the server has been checked against the current IETF specifications, but there are some deviations like mandating PKCE every client, confidential included, which exceeds what the spec requires.
Specs implemented:
* [draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1/) — OAuth 2.1 consolidation draft
* [RFC6749](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749) — The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework
* [RFC6750](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6750) — Bearer Token Usage
* [RFC7009](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7009) — Token Revocation
* [RFC7636](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7636) — PKCE (S256 only, no `plain` fallback)
* [RFC7662](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7662) — Token Introspection
* [RFC8414](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8414) — Authorization Server Metadata (discovery)
* [RFC8628](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8628) — Device Authorization Grant
* [RFC8252](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8252) — OAuth for Native Apps (BCP 212)
* [RFC9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700) — OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice (BCP 240)
