# OAuth
Last Updated   September 24, 2026
Guide
Personal Access Tokens are great for scripts and tools you run yourself.
You create the token, you paste it into your own config, only you ever see it.
But if you want other people to use your application or tool then OAuth is the way to go.

...

Everything below builds on the same [scopes](https://docs.hardcover.app/api/graphql/actions) as a Personal Access Token,
and once you do an OAuth flow and get an OAuth Access Token it works exactly like a PAT with the API,
the difference is entirely in how you get it.

...

## How it works
OAuth allows for a secure handshake between the auth provider (Hardcover) and your application by using the user as the courier.
There are 2 flows for OAuth we support, the standard flow ( [RFC6749](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749) ) and device authorization grant ( [RFC8628](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8628) ).

...

### Standard flow
1. Your app generate 2 random strings, one is the `state` and the other is the `code_verifier` for PKCE that you then SHA256 hash to get the `code_challenge` .
2. Your app sends the user to the authorize endpoint with your `client_id` , `redirect_uri` the place the user gets sent to after they finish on hardcover, the random `state` , and the PKCE `code_challenge` , and `scope` which is a subset of your allowed scopes.
3.
The user sees your app’s name, icon, and the scopes you’re asking for, and approves or denies.
4. Hardcover redirects back to your `redirect_uri` with a short-lived `code` (plus your `state` value, and an `iss` parameter naming the issuer).
5. Your app exchanges that code along with the PKCE `code_verifier` you generated in step 1 at the token endpoint for an access token and a refresh token.
6. Use the access token as a Bearer token against the API, exactly like a PAT.
This is the authorization code flow with PKCE, which we require every client use regardless of type.
There’s no separate “simpler” flow for a trusted client (and also no implicit grant).
So PKCE ( `code_challenge_method=S256` ) is required on every request, confidential clients included, it isn’t just for public clients.
Tip
Different clients can have slight differences from the flow described above, as it is the general steps for when you are a website, either SPA or SSR. For other types clients you will have to do some extra steps.
Desktop and CLI apps have to start a webserver and bind to a random localhost port after step 1 to catch the user when they return on the `redirect_uri` .
Hardcover accepts any port on localhost (and other loopback addresses) so you don’t have to worry if the port you wanted is already in use and you have to register another.

...

Mobile apps can set a custom scheme (instead of https) for the `redirect_uri` that will launch their app to collect the user. And when sending the user to Hardcover they can use a webview.
Note
Check that `state` matches what you sent in step 2 (this is what makes the flow safe from CSRF),
and check that `iss` equals `https://api.hardcover.app` before treating `code` or `state` as valid.
Hardcover only has one authorization server today, but the `iss` check is what stops a malicious server from ever being able to hand your app a code that gets redeemed at the wrong place (a “mix-up” attack ( [RFC9207](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9207) )).

...

### Device Authorization Grant
1. Your app requests a Device Auth Grant to start with your `client_id` , and optionally `scope` if you want a subset of your allowed scopes.
2. Hardcover gives your app a json object (see table below) that has info on where to send the user, what code the user should enter and how often you should poll.
3.
Your app starts polling the device auth endpoint at `interval` seconds until `expires_in` elapses, and sends the `device_code` so hardcover knows which request is being discussed.
4.
Your app tells the user to go to `verification_uri` ( [hardcover.app/link](https://hardcover.app/link) ) and enter `user_code` (it will be in the format of “ABCD-1234”), additionally you can turn `verification_uri_complete` into a QR code, that will take the user and prefill the code for them.
5. After the user enters the code the user sees your app’s name, icon, and the scopes you’re asking for, and approves or denies.
6.
Hardcover will respond to one of your poll requests with the access token and refresh token.
7. Use the access token as a Bearer token against the API, exactly like a PAT.
Response for device auth flow start (step 2)
| Field | Description |
| `device_code` | id you use to identify your polling requests |
| `user_code` | the code you tell the user to enter |
| `verification_uri` | where you tell the user to go |
| `verification_uri_complete` | a complete url you can turn to a QR that will prefill the code |
| `expires_in` | in seconds, how long you have to do the auth before giving up |
| `interval` | in seconds, how often you should poll |
Note
When turning `verification_uri_complete` into a QR code, make sure that you are still displaying the instructions using `verification_uri` and `user_code` in case the user can’t scan a QR code.
Caution

...

For the standard OAuth flow on public clients this is not as much of a issue, for websites Hardcover will only accept registered `redirect_uri` , so unless someone takes over your domain they can not start an OAuth flow in your name. But it can be an issue for CLI and desktop apps, so unless your app needs it don’t register a loopback address as an accepted `redirect_uri` .

...

## Which flow do I need?
| You’re building | Pick | Client type | Guide |
| A server-rendered app (Rails, Django, Node, PHP, etc.) or Backend-For-Frontend (BFF) server for an app, anything that runs on infrastructure you control | Web app (server-side) | Confidential: Gets a client secret, plus PKCE | [Confidential client guide](https://docs.hardcover.app/api/oauth/getting-started-server) |
| A React/Vue/Svelte app that runs in the user’s browser | Single-page app | Public: no secret, PKCE only | [SPA guide](https://docs.hardcover.app/api/oauth/getting-started-spa) |
| A mobile app, desktop app, CLI tool, or e-reader plugin | Mobile, desktop, or CLI | Public: no secret, PKCE only, Device Authorization Grant enabled, can have custom URI schemes in redirect | [Native / device guide](https://docs.hardcover.app/api/oauth/getting-started-device) |

...

### What is PKCE?
Section titled “What is PKCE?”
PKCE ( [RFC 7636](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7636) ) is an addition to the OAuth flow to make sure that the client that started the flow is the device that completed it.
By having the device make up a secret with at least 256 bits entropy ( `code_verifier` ) then send a SHA256 hashed version ( `code_challenge` ) of it to the server when starting the flow, the auth provider can be sure that only someone who can provide the code that hashes to the challenge it initially got is the correct device when doing the key exchange.

...

### Why should I disable Device Authorization Grant if I am not using it
Unlike the standard flows where even for Public apps the auth provider can only send the user to pre-approved `redirect_uri` s,
for Device Authorization Grant all you need is the apps public client id.
So if you don’t disable Device Auth Grant people will be able to take the client id that is embedded in your app, and in the standard flow is sent with the user, and start Auth flows with it in the name of your apps with whatever scopes have allowed for it.

...

## Endpoints
All of these (and the full set of grant types, scopes, and auth methods this server supports) are also published at the discovery document.
It is recommended that you make a call to discovery and read it at startup rather than hardcoding these if you can,
since if we ever have to change anything then your app can load in the new URLs automatically.
| Purpose | URL |
| Discovery | https://api.hardcover.app/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server |
| Token | `POST` https://api.hardcover.app/oauth2/token |
| Revoke | `POST` https://api.hardcover.app/oauth2/revoke |
| Introspect (confidential clients only) | `POST` https://api.hardcover.app/oauth2/introspect |
| Device authorization | `POST` https://api.hardcover.app/oauth2/device |
| Authorize (browser redirect) | https://hardcover.app/oauth2/authorize |
| Device verification (human-facing) | https://hardcover.app/link |

## Tokens
Section titled “Tokens”
Access and refresh tokens are opaque random strings, not JWTs. There’s nothing to decode client-side.
If you need to check whether a token is still valid, use the introspection endpoint (confidential clients only) or just try it against the API.
* **Access tokens** ( `hc_at_XXXXX` ) last 1 week and work exactly like a PAT for API requests.
* **Refresh tokens** ( `hc_rt_XXXXX` ) last 6 months, and **rotate on every use** .
Each refresh returns a new refresh token, and the one you just spent stops working.
If a refresh token ever gets used twice (yours got copied, or you’re retrying a request that actually succeeded),
the server treats it as a replay and revokes that token’s entire chain, making it so the user has to go through an OAuth flow again.
Your app should always save the newest refresh token and only ever use it once.

## Scopes
Section titled “Scopes”
OAuth apps use the same [scopes](https://docs.hardcover.app/api/graphql/actions) as Personal Access Tokens, but there are a some differences between them and PATs:
The scopes you list when registering your app are a cap, and are intersected with your requested scopes at consent time, that is then intersected with the user’s allowed scopes at request time.

...

When you make a request to the OAuth authorize endpoint you have to include the scopes you want, they are not implied from your allowed scopes.
But, it is possible to omit them when refreshing the token, you will then be issued a token with the same scopes as the last one.
You can also request any subset of the scopes the user consented to when refreshing without having to go through the OAuth flow again.

...

## Registering an app
| Field | What it’s for |
| Application type | Confidential vs. public, and can’t be changed later — see Which flow do I need . |
| Name | Shown to the user on the consent screen, and afterward in their list of connected apps. |
| Icon | Same as Name — consent screen and the connected apps list. |
| Description | Not currently shown at consent time — it only appears later, on the user’s connected apps list. Reserved for a future use (either added to the consent screen, or a future app directory style feature) — worth filling in for when that lands, even though it’s not surfaced yet. |
| Website URL | Shown as a link on the consent screen, right under your app’s name — it and the redirect host are the two things a user can actually verify, since `client_id` alone can be seen by anyone. |
| Redirect URIs | Where Hardcover sends the user back after they approve or deny. Must be `https` , except loopback addresses ( `127.0.0.1` , `[::1]` , `localhost` ) where it can be `http` — for local development or desktop apps. A custom URI scheme is possible for native apps. URIs are matched exactly — no wildcards or prefixes. |
| Device Authorization Grant toggle | Lets your app’s `client_id` be used at the device endpoint and `hardcover.app/link` . Off unless you turn it on (pre-checked for native apps, but still changeable). |
| Scopes this app may request | The ceiling described under Scopes above. Only ask for what you actually need, the app can request a subset of these at auth time, shown on the consent screen. |

...

## Consent and revoking access
Users manage every app they’ve connected from the [Authorized Apps](https://hardcover.app/account/api/authorized-apps) page.
Revoking an app there kills every token it holds for that user immediately, and clears their consent record — your app will need to send them through the authorize flow again from scratch, not just refresh.

...

## Storing tokens on the client
Section titled “Storing tokens on the client”

...

## Appearance in Authorized apps
* Active sessions are sessions where the Access Token is still valid and might be in use.
* Idle sessions are where the Access Token has expired, but the Refresh Token is still valid and can be used to reactivate the session.
On each of the sessions we store the last used User Agent and parse that to show a client name,
however it only parse out common user agents, and if it does not recognise the User Agent it will show up blank.
If you want your client to show correctly (e.g. ‘Softcover’ or ‘Hardcover.app for KOReader’) then reach out on discord!

...

## Compliance
Hardcover’s OAuth tries to be in compliance with the [OAuth 2.1 recommendations](https://oauth.net/2.1/) .
So the server has been checked against the current IETF specifications, but there are some deviations like mandating PKCE every client, confidential included, which exceeds what the spec requires.
Specs implemented:
* [draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1/) — OAuth 2.1 consolidation draft
* [RFC6749](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749) — The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework
* [RFC6750](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6750) — Bearer Token Usage
* [RFC7009](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7009) — Token Revocation
* [RFC7636](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7636) — PKCE (S256 only, no `plain` fallback)
* [RFC7662](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7662) — Token Introspection
* [RFC8414](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8414) — Authorization Server Metadata (discovery)
* [RFC8628](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8628) — Device Authorization Grant
* [RFC8252](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8252) — OAuth for Native Apps (BCP 212)
* [RFC9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700) — OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice (BCP 240)

# Searching for Content in the API
## Disclaimer:
Portions of this documentation may be auto-generated and may be incomplete or inaccurate. Currently this includes the schema relationship graph and field descriptions.

## What Can I Search For?
Section titled “What Can I Search For?”
Currently, you can search for authors, books, characters, lists, prompts, publishers, series, and users.
Additional search options will be added in the future.

...

The search API does not currently support filtering by parameters besides `query` , however you can
change which attributes (columns) are searched as well as changing sorting.

## Search Options
Section titled “Search Options”
Only `query` is required. If all other fields are blank, this will default to the same search as the Hardcover website when searching for a book.
* `query` * - The search term
* `query_type` - The type of content to search for one of (case-insensitive; default `book` )
+ `author`
+ `book`
+ `character`
+ `list`
+ `prompt`
+ `publisher`
+ `series`
+ `user`
* `per_page` - The number of results to return per page (default 25)
* `page` - The page number to return (default 1)
* `sort` - What attributes should the result be sorted by
* `fields` - Which attributes within the given `query_type` to include in the search
* `weights` - A comma separated list of numbers indicating weights to give each of the `fields` when calculating match
* `typos` - A comma separated list of numbers indicating the typo tolerance for each of the `fields` when calculating match (will show up in errors as `num_typos` )

...

## Available Fields
* `ids` - Array of `id` attributes for results in order
* `results` - Result objects returned from Typesense
* `query` - Passed in `query` , or default
* `query_type` - Passed in `query_type` , or default
* `page` - Passed in `page` , or default
* `per_page` - Passed in `per_page` , or default

## Example Searches
Section titled “Example Searches”

### Authors
Section titled “Authors”
The following fields are available in the returned object. You can also `sort` by any of these, or limit you search to specific field(s) using `fields` and `weights` .
* `alternate_names` - Alternative names for the author
* `books` - Titles of the top 5 most popular books by this author
* `books_count` - Number of books by this author
* `image` - Image object containing image URL, dimensions, color, etc.
* `name` - The name of the author
* `name_personal` - The personal name of the author
* `series_names` - The names of the different series the author has written
* `slug` - The URL slug of this author

#### Default Values
Section titled “Default Values”
When searching authors, we use the following default values.
* `fields` : `name,name_personal,alternate_names,series_names,books`
* `sort` : `_text_match:desc,books_count:desc`
* `weights` : `3,3,3,2,1`
* `typos` : `5`
* Query
* Try it yourself
Search Authors
```
query BooksByRowling { search ( query : " rowling " , query_type : " Author " , per_page : 5 , page : 1 ) { results } }
```

...

### Books
* `activities_count` - Number of activities for this book
* `alternative_titles` - Alternative titles for the book
* `audio_seconds` - Number of seconds for the default audiobook edition
* `author_names` - The name of the authors or contributors of the book
* `compilation` - Boolean if this book is a compilation
* `content_warnings` - Top 5 content warnings
* `contribution_types` - Array of contribution types for contributions
* `contributions` - Array of contribution objects
* `cover_color` - The extracted color of the book (ex: `red` , `green` )
* `description` - The description of the book
* `featured_series` - Object containing information about the series
* `featured_series_position` - Number indicating the featured series position
* `genres` - Top 5 genres
* `isbns` - The ISBNs of the book
* `lists_count` - Number of lists this book is on
* `has_audiobook` - Boolean if known to have an audiobook
* `has_ebook` - Boolean if known to have an ebook
* `moods` - Top 5 moods
* `pages` - Number of pages of the default physical edition
* `prompts_count` - Number of prompts this book is on
* `rating` - Hardcover average rating
* `ratings_count` - Number of Hardcover ratings
* `release_date_i` - The release date as an integer
* `release_year` - Date the book was published
* `reviews_count` - Number of Hardcover reviews
* `series_names` - The name of the series the book belongs to
* `slug` - The URL slug of the book
* `subtitle` - The subtitle of the book
* `tags` - Top 5 tags

Currently, you can search for authors, books, characters, lists, prompts, publishers, series, and users.

content.text: # creating-views Skill # Creating Views A view is one self-contained HTML page that the Amp web UI renders inline in your reply, in a sandboxed frame on the thread's own background that follows the reader's light or dark theme. Publish the page as a visual artifact, then embed it in your reply with Markdown image syntax: 1. Call the `artifact` tool with `action: "publish"`, `kind: "visual"`, `folder: "visuals"`, a short title, and the whole page as `content`. The content is HTML and nothing else: no Markdown and no code fence around it. 2. Put the returned `url` in your reply as an image, on its own line: `![Deep mode growth](URL)`. The reader sees the page there, and can open it as an artifact they can share. To show the view inside a document artifact, such as a report, put the same image line in the document's Markdown. ````markdown Deep mode is now Amp's second most used mode. ![Deep mode tripled in six weeks](https://ampcode.com/artifacts/visuals/deep-mode-growth-…) Most of the growth came from existing Smart users switching, not new users. ```` To change a view, publish the same artifact again with `edits` or new `content` and embed it again. Each publish replaces the page, so every embed of it shows the latest revision; publish a new artifact when the reader should keep the earlier version. Without the `artifact` tool, write the page in a fenced code block with the `amp-view` language tag instead, which renders the same way. The reader sees the view in place. Do not announce it or restate it in your text; write only what the view does not say. ## When to use a view Use a view when seeing answers the question faster than reading: - Data: a trend over time, a ranking, a distribution, or a comparison across more than about six values. - Systems: any diagram, such as an architecture, flowchart, sequence, state machine, timeline, race between callers, tree, or commit graph, including small static ones. - Derivations: how a number is computed, with inputs the reader can change. - Design: a quick UI experiment, such as a component or screen mockup, an interaction prototype, a layout wireframe, or two or three design directions side by side. - Any request to chart, plot, graph, visualize, diagram, mock up, prototype, sketch, try out a UI idea, or build a dashboard. Use Markdown instead for a short list, a table of a few rows, or one or two numbers. A view adds nothing to a code change summary; show the diff instead. ## The standard A view must look like it shipped with Amp: calm, quiet, and precise. Readers glance at it between other work, so it has one point, and that point is legible in one second. Everything else is gray and small so that one thing stands out. Restraint is the style: when in doubt, remove. Looking right is the easy part. Views fail far more often because the chart does not show what the title claims, so every view must also prove its point: - Before writing code, write the one sentence the reader should take away. For a chart it becomes the title; for a mockup or diagram it decides which state to open on. - Compute every number in the title from the data embedded in the view. Never quote a number the view does not contain, and never let a title rest on a default or placeholder value; in a calculator, generate the title from the current state. - Choose the encoding the claim needs. A claim about a multiple plots the multiple, a claim about a share draws the share, and "N% within X" draws a cumulative share. `reference/charts.md` covers this. - Make the default state show the point at 360px without any interaction. Open a stepper on the step that proves the title, color the path that matters before anyone clicks, and open a mockup on the state that decides the design. Screenshots, phones, and skimming readers only ever see the default state. - Say in a muted subtitle or caption what was measured, over what scope, and how the measure could mislead (a partial week, a known bias in the source, an assumption). ## How to build one 1. Write the takeaway sentence. 2. Read the reference for the kind of view, in this skill's `reference/` directory: - `charts.md` for charts, distributions, calculations, comparison and decision matrices, tables, and dashboards. - `ui-explorations.md` for mockups, prototypes, design options, interactive experiments, and wireframes. - `diagrams.md` for architecture diagrams, flowcharts, sequence diagrams, state machines, timelines, race timelines, trees, commit graphs, and step-through explainers. 3. Start from the closest example in `examples/`. Each is a complete view that follows this guide; reuse its structure and code, and replace its placeholder subject and data with yours. - `indexed-lines.html`: a line chart whose title states a multiple, plotted against each series' own baseline. - `highlighted-bars.html`: a ranking with one highlighted bar, a gray tail row, and shares at the bar ends. - `cumulative-share.html`: a hand-drawn distribution (cumulative share on a log axis) with a pointer and keyboard readout. - `calculation.html`: a derivation ledger, one term per row, with inputs to change, a computed title, and the marginal cost. - `decision-matrix.html`: a weighted decision with sliders, a title computed from state, and the smallest change that flips the pick. - `design-options.html`: a UI exploration with today's behavior as a baseline, three directions, a stress condition, and working actions. - `flowchart.html`: a flowchart or state diagram that colors the path the title is about and reflows from a row to a column on phones. - `sequence.html`: a sequence diagram with a synced ledger of who holds what after each step. - `race-timeline.html`: a timeline of two concurrent callers on one time axis, with the moment the race breaks marked and the fix behind a switch. - `tree.html`: a file tree as an indented outline that opens only the path to the files the title names, with WAI-ARIA tree keys. 4. Check it as described in "Check before sending". ## The frame - The view is as wide as the reply column: about 720px on desktop and 360px on phones. Design for both. - Its height fits the document, so the whole view shows in the reply without scrolling inside it, and the reader can open it full screen. Aim for under 600px; past that, cut or split it into two views. Never size anything from the frame's height (`vh` units, `height: 100%` on `html` or `body`): the frame grows to fit the page, so such a page keeps growing. - There is no network: every request is blocked. Inline all CSS, JS, images (as data URLs), and data. Chart libraries and web fonts cannot load. - There are no popups, storage, or form submission. Clicks on `http(s)` links ask the reader first. Hover, clicks, and keys work inside the frame. Nothing can draw outside it. - Keep the page under 100 KB; aggregate data before embedding it. - Wrap your script in a block (`{ … }`). Top-level `const top`, `name`, or `status` collide with browser globals and stop the script. ## Tokens Amp sets these on `:root`. They update live when the reader switches theme. Use them for every color; never write a hex value for anything Amp-colored. | Token | Use | | ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | | `--background` | The thread background, also under the view | | `--foreground` | Primary text, the one thing that matters | | `--muted-foreground` | Secondary text, labels, axes | | `--border` | Hairline rules, rings, the zero baseline | | `--grid` | Chart gridlines, fainter than `--border` | | `--card` | A 2–3% wash for a surface that stands for a real object | | `--muted` | A 7% wash for hover, selection, neutral fills | | `--chart-1` … `--chart-6` | Data series, in order | | `--chart-context` | Gray for context series | | `--series-1` … `--series-10` | The Amp team's dashboard palette, for many parts | | `--success`, `--warning`, `--destructive` | Status marks only | | `--link` | Links | | `--radius` | 8px | | `--font-sans`, `--font-mono` | System sans and mono | The base stylesheet sets the background, `--foreground` text, `--font-sans` at 13px/20px, and `body { margin: 0 }`. It does not restyle `a`, `b`, `strong`, or `h1` to `h4`, which render as browser blue links, bold, and large headings; use the kit's text classes instead of these elements. ## The kit Every view loads Amp's view kit: Amp's own components as CSS classes, Lucide icons, and `window.ui` for charts and motion. Build with it first; write your own CSS only for what it lacks. It is what makes a view look like Amp instead of a generic web page. Text and layout: - `.ui-header` wraps `.ui-title` (13px, 500) and `.ui-sub` (12px muted) with 16px below. Every view opens with one, prototypes included. - `.ui-label` (12px muted), `.ui-caption` (11px muted), `.ui-muted`, `.ui-num` (tabular), `.ui-big` (20px headline number), `.ui-mono`, `code`. - `.ui-stack` (grid, gap from `--gap`, default 12px; empty children collapse), `.ui-row` (flex, centered, gap 8px), `.ui-rule` (hairline). content.content: # creating-views Skill # Creating Views A view is one self-contained HTML page that the Amp web UI renders inline in your reply, in a sandboxed frame on the thread's own background that follows the reader's light or dark theme. Publish the page as a visual artifact, then embed it in your reply with Markdown image syntax: 1. Call the `artifact` tool with `action: "publish"`, `kind: "visual"`, `folder: "visuals"`, a short title, and the whole page as `content`. The content is HTML and nothing else: no Markdown and no code fence around it. 2. Put the returned `url` in your reply as an image, on its own line: `![Deep mode growth](URL)`. The reader sees the page there, and can open it as an artifact they can share. To show the view inside a document artifact, such as a report, put the same image line in the document's Markdown. ````markdown Deep mode is now Amp's second most used mode. ![Deep mode tripled in six weeks](https://ampcode.com/artifacts/visuals/deep-mode-growth-…) Most of the growth came from existing Smart users switching, not new users. ```` To change a view, publish the same artifact again with `edits` or new `content` and embed it again. Each publish replaces the page, so every embed of it shows the latest revision; publish a new artifact when the reader should keep the earlier version. Without the `artifact` tool, write the page in a fenced code block with the `amp-view` language tag instead, which renders the same way. The reader sees the view in place. Do not announce it or restate it in your text; write only what the view does not say. ## When to use a view Use a view when seeing answers the question faster than reading: - Data: a trend over time, a ranking, a distribution, or a comparison across more than about six values. - Systems: any diagram, such as an architecture, flowchart, sequence, state machine, timeline, race between callers, tree, or commit graph, including small static ones. - Derivations: how a number is computed, with inputs the reader can change. - Design: a quick UI experiment, such as a component or screen mockup, an interaction prototype, a layout wireframe, or two or three design directions side by side. - Any request to chart, plot, graph, visualize, diagram, mock up, prototype, sketch, try out a UI idea, or build a dashboard. Use Markdown instead for a short list, a table of a few rows, or one or two numbers. A view adds nothing to a code change summary; show the diff instead. ## The standard A view must look like it shipped with Amp: calm, quiet, and precise. Readers glance at it between other work, so it has one point, and that point is legible in one second. Everything else is gray and small so that one thing stands out. Restraint is the style: when in doubt, remove. Looking right is the easy part. Views fail far more often because the chart does not show what the title claims, so every view must also prove its point: - Before writing code, write the one sentence the reader should take away. For a chart it becomes the title; for a mockup or diagram it decides which state to open on. - Compute every number in the title from the data embedded in the view. Never quote a number the view does not contain, and never let a title rest on a default or placeholder value; in a calculator, generate the title from the current state. - Choose the encoding the claim needs. A claim about a multiple plots the multiple, a claim about a share draws the share, and "N% within X" draws a cumulative share. `reference/charts.md` covers this. - Make the default state show the point at 360px without any interaction. Open a stepper on the step that proves the title, color the path that matters before anyone clicks, and open a mockup on the state that decides the design. Screenshots, phones, and skimming readers only ever see the default state. - Say in a muted subtitle or caption what was measured, over what scope, and how the measure could mislead (a partial week, a known bias in the source, an assumption). ## How to build one 1. Write the takeaway sentence. 2. Read the reference for the kind of view, in this skill's `reference/` directory: - `charts.md` for charts, distributions, calculations, comparison and decision matrices, tables, and dashboards. - `ui-explorations.md` for mockups, prototypes, design options, interactive experiments, and wireframes. - `diagrams.md` for architecture diagrams, flowcharts, sequence diagrams, state machines, timelines, race timelines, trees, commit graphs, and step-through explainers. 3. Start from the closest example in `examples/`. Each is a complete view that follows this guide; reuse its structure and code, and replace its placeholder subject and data with yours. - `indexed-lines.html`: a line chart whose title states a multiple, plotted against each series' own baseline. - `highlighted-bars.html`: a ranking with one highlighted bar, a gray tail row, and shares at the bar ends. - `cumulative-share.html`: a hand-drawn distribution (cumulative share on a log axis) with a pointer and keyboard readout. - `calculation.html`: a derivation ledger, one term per row, with inputs to change, a computed title, and the marginal cost. - `decision-matrix.html`: a weighted decision with sliders, a title computed from state, and the smallest change that flips the pick. - `design-options.html`: a UI exploration with today's behavior as a baseline, three directions, a stress condition, and working actions. - `flowchart.html`: a flowchart or state diagram that colors the path the title is about and reflows from a row to a column on phones. - `sequence.html`: a sequence diagram with a synced ledger of who holds what after each step. - `race-timeline.html`: a timeline of two concurrent callers on one time axis, with the moment the race breaks marked and the fix behind a switch. - `tree.html`: a file tree as an indented outline that opens only the path to the files the title names, with WAI-ARIA tree keys. 4. Check it as described in "Check before sending". ## The frame - The view is as wide as the reply column: about 720px on desktop and 360px on phones. Design for both. - Its height fits the document, so the whole view shows in the reply without scrolling inside it, and the reader can open it full screen. Aim for under 600px; past that, cut or split it into two views. Never size anything from the frame's height (`vh` units, `height: 100%` on `html` or `body`): the frame grows to fit the page, so such a page keeps growing. - There is no network: every request is blocked. Inline all CSS, JS, images (as data URLs), and data. Chart libraries and web fonts cannot load. - There are no popups, storage, or form submission. Clicks on `http(s)` links ask the reader first. Hover, clicks, and keys work inside the frame. Nothing can draw outside it. - Keep the page under 100 KB; aggregate data before embedding it. - Wrap your script in a block (`{ … }`). Top-level `const top`, `name`, or `status` collide with browser globals and stop the script. ## Tokens Amp sets these on `:root`. They update live when the reader switches theme. Use them for every color; never write a hex value for anything Amp-colored. | Token | Use | | ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | | `--background` | The thread background, also under the view | | `--foreground` | Primary text, the one thing that matters | | `--muted-foreground` | Secondary text, labels, axes | | `--border` | Hairline rules, rings, the zero baseline | | `--grid` | Chart gridlines, fainter than `--border` | | `--card` | A 2–3% wash for a surface that stands for a real object | | `--muted` | A 7% wash for hover, selection, neutral fills | | `--chart-1` … `--chart-6` | Data series, in order | | `--chart-context` | Gray for context series | | `--series-1` … `--series-10` | The Amp team's dashboard palette, for many parts | | `--success`, `--warning`, `--destructive` | Status marks only | | `--link` | Links | | `--radius` | 8px | | `--font-sans`, `--font-mono` | System sans and mono | The base stylesheet sets the background, `--foreground` text, `--font-sans` at 13px/20px, and `body { margin: 0 }`. # UI explorations, prototypes, and experiments

A UI exploration exists to settle one design decision. It succeeds when the reader can pick a direction after trying it, not when it looks finished. `examples/design-options.html` is the pattern.

## Frame the decision

- The title asks the question the exploration settles: "Where should a failed attachment upload show?" The subtitle names the directions and tells the reader what to try.
- Show today's shipped behavior first, labeled "Today", so every direction is judged against what exists. Skip it only for a surface that does not exist yet.
- Offer at most three directions, each different on one named axis (placement, density, interaction model, how much it interrupts). If two directions differ only in color or copy, they are one direction. Name each by what it does ("On chip", "Block send"), not "Option A".
- Put one muted trade-off line under the switcher that changes with the selection: what this direction costs, not only what it gains.
- When you rejected a direction while designing, say so in one "Also considered" line with the reason, instead of building it.
- When the user asks for many options, group them by axis with one verdict per group, show them as a list beside one stage that renders the selected option, and narrow to two or three in the next round.

## Show the deciding state

- Open on the state that decides the design, not the empty or happy state: the error, the long title, the open menu, the narrow width.
- Add a second control, outside the mock, for the condition that stresses each direction ("1 file failed", "1 of 3 failed", "Offline"). Every direction must handle every condition.
- Pin hover-only UI (a tooltip, a menu, a row's actions) open in the default state, because screenshots and phones never hover.
- Crop to the region that matters inside one surface for the window. A composer change needs the composer and the last message, not the whole app. Crop a phone frame to its content instead of drawing the full device.
- Stack full-width directions vertically or behind a switcher; place small components side by side at the same scale.

## Make the actions work

- Keep all state in one object, render the whole mock from it, and re-render on every change. Never patch the DOM piecemeal.
- Make the actions that decide the design real buttons that change the state: Retry, Remove, Send, Undo. A mock where the deciding action does nothing cannot settle the question.
- After a re-render, move focus back to the control the reader used.
- Give targets at least 24px, and 44px when the mock is of a touch surface.
- Offer Reset, and replay or slow motion when timing is the question (a toast's duration, a transition). Do not loop an animation unless the shipped animation loops.
- Use the kit's controls for the exploration's own switcher and conditions, and keep them visually separate from the mock so the reader never confuses the two.

## Mocking Amp

- Read the surface's DESIGN.md and the real component source before drawing. When the source and this skill's type rules differ, the source wins inside the mock.
- Reuse Amp's anatomy from the kit: `.ui-user-msg`, `.ui-tool-row`, `.ui-composer`, `.ui-chip`, `.ui-btn`. Tool and event rows are plain muted text with no icons. While the agent is running, the composer's send button shows Stop.
- Use Title Case for titles and buttons inside the mock when Amp does; the exploration's own labels stay in sentence case.
- Use real copy and realistic data: real file names, real error messages, plausible lengths. Placeholder text hides the problems the exploration is for, such as wrapping and truncation.
- When mocking another product, use its real colors and type from its code.
- For a status or notification card (an approval request, a finished run, an error), mock the surface it appears on, show the states it moves through (pending, done, failed) behind a switch, and use the real copy for each.

## Experiments and calculators

An experiment lets the reader change an input and see a consequence: a pricing calculator, a timeout tuner, a layout density slider.

- Open on the observed or agreed values, not round placeholders.
- Compute the title from the current state, so it always states the current answer ("At 40 requests per second, p95 stays under 200 ms").
- Show the output the reader cares about large enough to follow, and animate numbers with `ui.tween` so changes are visible.
- Mark the inputs that are assumptions, and the range over which the model holds.
- When there is a threshold, say where it is: "Above 64 the queue never drains."

## Sketches and wireframes

When the question is layout or flow rather than visual detail, draw a wireframe instead of a polished mockup:

- Content is gray bars (`.ui-wire`); containers are hairline rings (`.ui-wire-box`). Write real text only where it matters (button names, file names, the label that is in question).
- Color only what carries meaning in the sketch, such as diff green and red or the primary button.
- Number the decisions with `.ui-note` markers, list the notes beside or below the sketches, and highlight a note's region in every variant on hover.
- Show two or three variants side by side at the same scale, each with a short name.
- Keep the geometry crisp. No hand-drawn wobble, handwriting fonts, or fake paper textures.

# Richer metadata: feasibility

**Verdict:** Feasible, with **Hardcover as the source** and **no Goodreads integration**. About half the experience (author and series pages over your own library) needs no external data at all and can ship first.

![Mockup: book, author and series pages](https://ampcode.com/artifacts/visuals/richer-metadata-book-author-and-series-pages-3f10d7fb-4560-45d5-8afe-e6edbcd7cb44)

## Sources

| Source | Access | Author pages | Series | Similar books | Genres / moods / rating | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Hardcover** | GraphQL, needs a token (PAT or OAuth). Free: 5,000 req/day, 60/min, burst 10 | Bio, photo, dates, full bibliography | Yes, with positions (`book_series`) | Yes: `cached_similar_book_ids` (~100, ranked, refreshed weekly) | Top 5 genres, moods, tags; avg rating and reader counts | **Use** |
| Goodreads | Public API closed to new keys since Dec 2020. Only scraping is left | – | – | – | – | **Skip.** Scraping is against their ToS and is what killed Readarr's metadata. Hardcover's `book_mappings` / `links` can give a "View on Goodreads" link instead |
| Open Library (already integrated) | Keyless | Bibliography exists but noisy (Le Guin: 262 "works", first page was Spanish/Portuguese translations) | No | No | Subjects only, multilingual and noisy | Keep for matching; weak for discovery |
| Google Books (already integrated) | Needs a key | No | No | No | Categories, sparse | No help here |

What I verified: Open Library calls (live). Hardcover facts come from its docs (updated Oct 2026); an unauthenticated call returns 400, and there's no token in this orb, so I haven't hit it with real queries.

## What each feature needs

| Feature | Data needed | Works offline? |
|---|---|---|
| Click author → their books in your library | Nothing new; group by author name | Yes |
| Click series → series in your library, in order | Nothing new for books that already have `series` set | Yes |
| Series for books that lack it | Hardcover `book_series` written into `books.matched` | After matching |
| Author page: bio and "Not in your library" | A Hardcover author id for the book's author | Cached |
| Similar books (library + Market) | A Hardcover book id, then one request for the similar list | Cached |
| Genres, moods, rating | A Hardcover book id | Cached |
| "Get it" for a book not in your library | Existing Market search with `?q=<title> <author>` | Needs a source |

Linking to the library uses `bookKeys()` in `src/lib/market/merge.ts`: ISBN-13 first, then title + author surname. The Market already uses it to merge results, so "In library" here means the same thing as it does on the Market page.

## How it fits the code

- **Hardcover as a third `MetadataProvider`** (`src/lib/metadata/hardcover.ts`). The plan already lists it. Its search fills `series` and `seriesIndex`, which neither current provider can. `fetchJson` needs a POST variant for GraphQL.
- **Remember the provider's ids, not just its fields.** Today a match only keeps `matched.source = { provider, id }` for the most recent match, and **Revert** deletes it. Similar books, author pages and genres need a durable Hardcover book id (plus author ids) per book.
- **Cache display-only data instead of storing it.** Rating, genres, the similar list and author bios change over time and aren't fields anyone edits. Fetch them lazily when a book or author page opens, cache in SQLite with a TTL (7 days, matching Hardcover's refresh), and show the page without them when offline.
- **Budget:** lazy fetching costs about 2 requests per page view, and the cache makes repeat views free. An optional bulk "Match library" pass for 1,000 books is about 2,000 requests, roughly 35 min at 60/min, which fits the free daily cap.
- **New routes:** `/authors/$name` and `/series/$name`. Make the author and series on the book page into links.

## Decisions needed (one-way doors)

1. **Storing ids durably** needs a schema change shipped to installs: a `book_identities (book_id, provider, external_id)` table plus a metadata cache table. A stopgap that needs no migration is to keep ids in the `matched` JSON, but **Revert** would lose them. **Recommendation:** new tables.
2. **Hardcover auth.**
   - **Option A: `HARDCOVER_TOKEN` env var (PAT).** Same pattern as `GOOGLE_BOOKS_API_KEY`; fastest to build.
   - **Option B: OAuth device flow.** Admin clicks "Connect Hardcover" in Settings and enters a code at hardcover.app/link. Hardcover recommends this ("never ask a user to paste a PAT"). It needs a **Bookserve public client registered with Hardcover** (Harris to do), and the refresh token has to be stored and rotated in the data dir.

   **Recommendation:** A to prototype, B before release.
3. **New external dependency.** Hardcover stays optional: with no token, the library-only author and series pages still work.

## Terms worth knowing

- **Allowed:** aggregate data (average rating, reader counts) for a self-hosted personal install, labeled as Hardcover data.
- **Not allowed:** user-owned data (reviews, lists) in public or commercial products. We don't need it.
- **Unstable API:** Hardcover says the API is "heavily in flux" and tokens may be reset during the beta. Keep the provider isolated, and fail soft on 401/429.
- **Images:** they're user-uploaded. The DMCA warning only applies to public sites; Bookserve already caches covers locally.

## Suggested phases

1. **Library-only author and series pages** (no network, no schema change). Author and series become links.
2. **Hardcover match provider** behind `HARDCOVER_TOKEN`. Fills series, plus the other fields it already supports.
3. **Ids + cache tables (migration)**, then on the book page: genres/moods, rating, "More by", and "Similar", each split into In library and Market.
4. **Author page** with bio and the full bibliography, and OAuth device-flow connect in Settings.

content.text:
Yes, this is feasible if we build it on Hardcover. Goodreads isn't an option: it stopped issuing API keys in December 2020, and scraping it is against its terms. Scraping-based Goodreads metadata is also what broke Readarr. Hardcover covers everything you described: author pages with bio and bibliography, series with positions, about 100 ranked similar books per title, and genres, moods and ratings.

![Mockup: book, author and series pages](https://ampcode.com/artifacts/visuals/richer-metadata-book-author-and-series-pages-3f10d7fb-4560-45d5-8afe-e6edbcd7cb44)

**What I found:**
- **About half needs no new data.** Clicking an author or series to see those books in your library can ship now. It works offline and needs no schema change.
- **Hardcover fills our biggest gap: series.** Neither Open Library nor Google Books returns usable series today, and Hardcover returns series with each book's position. It would slot in as a third provider next to the existing two.
- **Library vs. Market:** for "More by" and "Similar", we'd mark which books you already have using the matching the Market already does (ISBN first, then title and author). For a book you don't have, "Get it" would open the existing Market search for it.
- **Open Library isn't good enough for discovery.** I checked it live: Le Guin has 262 "works", and the first page was all Spanish and Portuguese translations. Its subjects are mixed-language and noisy, and it has no similar books.
- **Request budget:** Hardcover's free plan allows 5,000 requests a day and 60 a minute. Fetching only when a page opens, cached for 7 days, stays well within that. Matching a 1,000-book library in bulk would take about 35 minutes.
- **Not yet tested against Hardcover itself:** without a token it rejects requests, so its details come from its docs (updated October 2026).

**Two decisions for you, both hard to undo:**
1. **Schema change:** similar books, author pages and genres need each book's Hardcover id kept permanently, plus a cache table. Today a match keeps only one id, and "Revert to file metadata" deletes it. I recommend two new tables, which means a migration shipped to installs.
2. **How users connect Hardcover:** I'd prototype with a `HARDCOVER_TOKEN` environment variable (same pattern as the Google Books key). Before release I'd switch to Hardcover's device-code sign-in, where an admin enters a code at hardcover.app/link. That needs you to register Bookserve as an app with Hardcover.

The full write-up has the source comparison, how it fits the code, the terms that matter and a 4-phase plan: [Richer metadata: feasibility](https://ampcode.com/artifacts/richer-metadata-feasibility-hardcover-goodreads-1b000711-40a8-48b6-860b-66aae6bc9d89). I haven't changed any code.

content.text:
**Does it need an API key, and what are the limits?**

Yes, every Hardcover request needs a token. An unauthenticated request just returns 400. The limits that matter:

- **Rate limits:** 5,000 requests a day, 60 a minute, and at most 10 back-to-back. A 429 tells you how long to wait. This is the free plan, and the limit applies to the token, not the server's IP.
- **Token lifetime:**
  - A personal token you paste in lasts as long as you set when creating it.
  - The sign-in (OAuth) flow gives a token that lasts 1 week. It renews itself for up to 6 months, and each renewal is single-use.
  - Hardcover says the API is in beta and it may reset tokens without notice, so we have to handle an expired or revoked token gracefully.
- **Speed and terms:** searches time out after 2 seconds. The terms say you can't use the data to train public or commercial AI models. Neither affects us.

With a cache in front, 5,000 a day is plenty. A book page costs about 2 requests the first time and nothing after that for a week.

**One Hardcover account per server, or one per user?**

One per server. An admin connects it once in Settings.

- Everything this feature uses (book details, series, authors, similar books, genres, ratings) is public catalog data. It's the same no matter whose account fetches it.
- Matching is already admin-only, and the cache is shared, so one person opening a book page pays for everyone.
- Making every user connect would add work for each user and wouldn't change what anyone sees.

Per-user accounts only make sense for a different, personal feature, like syncing your reading status or ratings to your own Hardcover shelves. That could be added later as an optional link per user, and it wouldn't change the server-wide setup.

**Required or optional?**

Optional. Bookserve's project guidelines already settle this: online lookups are a feature, and the app must keep working offline or when a provider is down. Making a self-hosted server depend on a sign-up with a third party would also be a hard sell.

Making it required wouldn't remove the fallback anyway. Even with Hardcover connected, the server will be offline sometimes, hit a 429, have its token reset, or hold books that never matched. The "no Hardcover data" case has to work either way.

**Does that mean maintaining two versions?**

Not if the library is always the base and Hardcover only adds to it:

- **Author page:** always lists your books by that author. With Hardcover, it adds a bio and a "Not in your library" row.
- **Series page:** always shows your books in order. With Hardcover, it fills in the missing volumes.
- **Book page:** always shows what we show today, plus clickable author and series. With Hardcover, it adds genres, rating and "Similar".

Each Hardcover section hides itself when it has no data, the same way the description and Pages already do. So it's one page with optional sections, not two versions of it, and testing the fallback just means checking that a section stays hidden.

The duplication risk comes from building a page that only exists when Hardcover is connected, like an author page backed entirely by Hardcover next to a separate library one. Avoid that, and keep all Hardcover code in one module so its API changes don't spread through the app.

So my recommendation is: one server-wide connection, optional, and the library-only pages first. Hardcover then adds sections on top without forking anything.

I'm making DiscoverRow generic over `T extends DiscoverBook` so the cast in the series view goes away. I'm also weighing a small inconsistency: library books that Hardcover matched but that aren't tagged with the series in the library. They fall out of both "In your library" and "missing." I'm leaning toward accepting that, though including those library ids is an option.

I'm working out how the series page should show books that Hardcover matched but that aren't tagged with the series in the library. Right now the book page sends the user to the series page, which then reports "No books" in the library even though they just came from one of those books, so that's a visible bug. My plan is to have the discover series lookup also return the matching library cards by id, and have the UI merge them into the library list, deduped and ordered by position. The author page doesn't have this problem, since the library author string already lets it find the book.
